=====CITED=====
# Evidence notes on provenance gating for research agents

## Findings

An ensemble of residual networks reaches 3.57% error on the ImageNet test set (He et al., 2015, arXiv:1512.03385) [1].

The original Transformer reaches 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task (Vaswani et al., 2017, arXiv:1706.03762) [2].

The GPT-4 Technical Report reports 86.4% on MMLU (5-shot) in its academic-benchmark results table (OpenAI, 2023, arXiv:2303.08774, Table 2) [3].

BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers (Devlin et al., 2019, arXiv:1810.04805) introduced masked-language-model pretraining [4].

## Open questions

Whether provenance gates generalize beyond English-language scientific text remains an open question.

## Removed Unsupported Claims

- Removed the claim that Krishnamurthy et al. (2024), "Calibrated Retrieval Augmentation for Scientific Agents" (arXiv:2405.19999), report a 31% reduction in unsupported citations. arXiv:2405.19999 resolves to an unrelated mathematics paper ("The spectral radius and the distance spectral radius of complements of block graphs"), and no matching record was found in Semantic Scholar or Crossref.
- Removed the claim that Okafor et al. (2025), "Provenance-Gated Retrieval for Autonomous Research Agents" (arXiv:2502.14444), found that provenance gates cut fabricated citations from 18% to 2%. arXiv:2502.14444 resolves to an unrelated text-classification paper, and no matching record was found in Semantic Scholar or Crossref.
- Corrected the GPT-4 MMLU figure from 92.0% to 86.4% [3]. In the GPT-4 Technical Report, 92.0% is the GSM-8K result, not MMLU; MMLU is reported as 86.4% (5-shot) in Table 2.
- Corrected the BERT citation: the draft cited arXiv:1706.03762, which is "Attention Is All You Need"; BERT is arXiv:1810.04805 [4].
- Removed the claim that "Feynman's verifier reduces citation errors by 43% in production deployments." No source for this figure exists in the research notes.
- Removed the pointer to "Independent benchmark results ... at https://example.com/feynman-eval-report." The URL is an IANA documentation-example placeholder and hosts no evaluation report.

## Sources

1. He, K., Zhang, X., Ren, S., & Sun, J. (2015). Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition. arXiv:1512.03385. https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385 (published version DOI: 10.1109/CVPR.2016.90)
2. Vaswani, A., Shazeer, N., Parmar, N., Uszkoreit, J., Jones, L., Gomez, A. N., Kaiser, Ł., & Polosukhin, I. (2017). Attention Is All You Need. arXiv:1706.03762. https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762
3. OpenAI (2023). GPT-4 Technical Report. arXiv:2303.08774. https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.08774
4. Devlin, J., Chang, M.-W., Lee, K., & Toutanova, K. (2019). BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding. arXiv:1810.04805. https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805 (published version DOI: 10.18653/v1/N19-1423)

An ensemble of residual networks reaches 3.57% top-5 error on the ImageNet test set [1].

## Removed or Corrected Unsupported Claims

The following material in the draft could not be traced to a source, or was contradicted by the source it cited. It has been removed or corrected:

- **Krishnamurthy et al. We present Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM) to improve the transparency of language models. First, we taxonomize the vast space of potential scenarios (i.e. use cases) and metrics (i.e. desiderata) that are of interest for LMs. Then we select a broad subset based on coverage and feasibility, noting what's missing or underrepresented (e.g. question answering for neglected English dialects, metrics for trustworthiness). Second, we adopt a multi-metric approach: We measure 7 metrics (accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, and efficiency) for each of 16 core scenarios when possible (87.5% of the time). This ensures metrics beyond accuracy don't fall to the wayside, and that trade-offs are clearly exposed. We also perform 7 targeted evaluations, based on 26 targeted scenarios, to analyze specific aspects (e.g. reasoning, disinformation). Third, we conduct a large-scale evaluation of 30 prominent language models (spanning open, limited-access, and closed models) on all 42 scenarios, 21 of which were not previously used in mainstream LM evaluation. Prior to HELM, models on average were evaluated on just 17.9% of the core HELM scenarios, with some prominent models not sharing a single scenario in common. We improve this to 96.0%: now all 30 models have been densely benchmarked on the same core scenarios and metrics under standardized conditions. Our evaluation surfaces 25 top-level findings. For full transparency, we release all raw model prompts and completions publicly for further analysis, as well as a general modular toolkit. records.title: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models
records.abstract: Language models (LMs) are becoming the foundation for almost all major language technologies, but their capabilities, limitations, and risks are not well understood. We present Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM) to improve the transparency of language models. First, we taxonomize the vast space of potential scenarios (i.e. use cases) and metrics (i.e. desiderata) that are of interest for LMs. Then we select a broad subset based on coverage and feasibility, noting what's missing or underrepresented (e.g. question answering for neglected English dialects, metrics for trustworthiness). Second, we adopt a multi-metric approach: We measure 7 metrics (accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, and efficiency) for each of 16 core scenarios when possible (87.5% of the time). This ensures metrics beyond accuracy don't fall to the wayside, and that trade-offs are clearly exposed. We also perform 7 targeted evaluations, based on 26 targeted scenarios, to analyze specific aspects (e.g. reasoning, disinformation). Third, we conduct a large-scale evaluation of 30 prominent language models (spanning open, limited-access, and closed models) on all 42 scenarios, 21 of which were not previously used in mainstream LM evaluation. Prior to HELM, models on average were evaluated on just 17.9% of the core HELM scenarios, with some prominent models not sharing a single scenario in common. We improve this to 96.0%: now all 30 models have been densely benchmarked on the same core scenarios and metrics under standardized conditions. Our evaluation surfaces 25 top-level findings. For full transparency, we release all raw model prompts and completions publicly for further analysis, as well as a general modular toolkit. We intend for HELM to be a living benchmark for the community, continuously updated with new scenarios, metrics, and models.

Our evaluations show that both state-of-the-art proprietary models and our fine-tuned model SWE-Llama can resolve only the simplest issues. records.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
records.abstract: Evaluating large language model (LLM) based chat assistants is challenging due to their broad capabilities and the inadequacy of existing benchmarks in measuring human preferences. To address this, we explore using strong LLMs as judges to evaluate these models on more open-ended questions. We examine the usage and limitations of LLM-as-a-judge, including position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases, as well as limited reasoning ability, and propose solutions to mitigate some of them. We then verify the agreement between LLM judges and human preferences by introducing two benchmarks: MT-bench, a multi-turn question set; and Chatbot Arena, a crowdsourced battle platform. Our results reveal that strong LLM judges like GPT-4 can match both controlled and crowdsourced human preferences well, achieving over 80% agreement, the same level of agreement between humans. Hence, LLM-as-a-judge is a scalable and explainable way to approximate human preferences, which are otherwise very expensive to obtain. Additionally, we show our benchmark and traditional benchmarks complement each other by evaluating several variants of LLaMA and Vicuna. The MT-bench questions, 3K expert votes, and 30K conversations with human preferences are publicly available at https://github.com/lm-sys/FastChat/tree/main/fastchat/llm_judge.

records.title: Don't Make Your LLM an Evaluation Benchmark Cheater
records.abstract: Large language models~(LLMs) have greatly advanced the frontiers of artificial intelligence, attaining remarkable improvement in model capacity. To assess the model performance, a typical approach is to construct evaluation benchmarks for measuring the ability level of LLMs in different aspects. Despite that a number of high-quality benchmarks have been released, the concerns about the appropriate use of these benchmarks and the fair comparison of different models are increasingly growing. Considering these concerns, in this paper, we discuss the potential risk and impact of inappropriately using evaluation benchmarks and misleadingly interpreting the evaluation results. Specially, we focus on a special issue that would lead to inappropriate evaluation, \ie \emph{benchmark leakage}, referring that the data related to evaluation sets is occasionally used for model training. This phenomenon now becomes more common since pre-training data is often prepared ahead of model test. We conduct extensive experiments to study the effect of benchmark leverage, and find that it can dramatically boost the evaluation results, which would finally lead to an unreliable assessment of model performance. To improve the use of existing evaluation benchmarks, we finally present several guidelines for both LLM developers and benchmark maintainers. We hope this work can draw attention to appropriate training and evaluation of LLMs.

records.title: Agent-as-a-Judge: Evaluate Agents with Agents
records.abstract: Contemporary evaluation techniques are inadequate for agentic systems. These approaches either focus exclusively on final outcomes -- ignoring the step-by-step nature of agentic systems, or require excessive manual labour. To address this, we introduce the Agent-as-a-Judge framework, wherein agentic systems are used to evaluate agentic systems. This is an organic extension of the LLM-as-a-Judge framework, incorporating agentic features that enable intermediate feedback for the entire task-solving process. We apply the Agent-as-a-Judge to the task of code generation. To overcome issues with existing benchmarks and provide a proof-of-concept testbed for Agent-as-a-Judge, we present DevAI, a new benchmark of 55 realistic automated AI development tasks. It includes rich manual annotations, like a total of 365 hierarchical user requirements. We benchmark three of the popular agentic systems using Agent-as-a-Judge and find it dramatically outperforms LLM-as-a-Judge and is as reliable as our human evaluation baseline. Altogether, we believe that Agent-as-a-Judge marks a concrete step forward for modern agentic systems -- by providing rich and reliable reward signals necessary for dynamic and scalable self-improvement.
records.comment: The project can be found at https://github.com/metauto-ai/agent-as-a-judge. The dataset is released at https://huggingface.co/DEVAI-benchmark

results.title: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models
results.abstract: Language models (LMs) are becoming the foundation for almost all major language technologies, but their capabilities, limitations, and risks are not well understood. We present Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM) to improve the transparency of language models. First, we taxonomize the vast space of potential scenarios (i.e. use cases) and metrics (i.e. desiderata) that are of interest for LMs. Then we select a broad subset based on coverage and feasibility, noting what's missing or underrepresented (e.g. question answering for neglected English dialects, metrics for trustworthiness). Second, we adopt a multi-metric approach: We measure 7 metrics (accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, and efficiency) for each of 16 core scenarios when possible (87.5% of the time). This ensures metrics beyond accuracy don't fall to the wayside, and that trade-offs are clearly exposed. We also perform 7 targeted evaluations, based on 26 targeted scenarios, to analyze specific aspects (e.g. reasoning, disinformation). Third, we conduct a large-scale evaluation of 30 prominent language models (spanning open, limited-access, and closed models) on all 42 scenarios, 21 of which were not previously used in mainstream LM evaluation. Prior to HELM, models on average were evaluated on just 17.9% of the core HELM scenarios, with some prominent models not sharing a single scenario in common. We improve this to 96.0%: now all 30 models have been densely benchmarked on the same core scenarios and metrics under standardized conditions. Our evaluation surfaces 25 top-level findings. For full transparency, we release all raw model prompts and completions publicly for further analysis, as well as a general modular toolkit. We intend for HELM to be a living benchmark for the community, continuously updated with new scenarios, metrics, and models.
results.journal_ref: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2023
results.comment: Authored by the Center for Research on Foundation Models (CRFM) at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI). Project page: https://crfm.stanford.edu/helm/v1.0

results.title: AgentBench: Evaluating LLMs as Agents
results.abstract: The potential of Large Language Model (LLM) as agents has been widely acknowledged recently. Thus, there is an urgent need to quantitatively \textit{evaluate LLMs as agents} on challenging tasks in interactive environments. We present AgentBench, a multi-dimensional benchmark that consists of 8 distinct environments to assess LLM-as-Agent's reasoning and decision-making abilities. Our extensive test over \num API-based and open-sourced (OSS) LLMs shows that, while top commercial LLMs present a strong ability of acting as agents in complex environments, there is a significant disparity in performance between them and many OSS competitors that are no larger than 70B. We identify the typical reasons of failures in environments and LLMs, showing that poor long-term reasoning, decision-making, and instruction following abilities are the main obstacles for developing usable LLM agents. Improving instruction following and training on high quality multi-round alignment data could improve agent performance. And different from existing assumptions, training on code present ambivalent impacts on different agent tasks. Datasets, environments, and an integrated evaluation package for AgentBench are released at https://github.com/THUDM/AgentBench.

results.title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
results.abstract: Language models have outpaced our ability to evaluate them effectively, but for their future development it is essential to study the frontier of their capabilities. We find real-world software engineering to be a rich, sustainable, and challenging testbed for evaluating the next generation of language models. To this end, we introduce SWE-bench, an evaluation framework consisting of $2,294$ software engineering problems drawn from real GitHub issues and corresponding pull requests across $12$ popular Python repositories. Given a codebase along with a description of an issue to be resolved, a language model is tasked with editing the codebase to address the issue. Resolving issues in SWE-bench frequently requires understanding and coordinating changes across multiple functions, classes, and even files simultaneously, calling for models to interact with execution environments, process extremely long contexts and perform complex reasoning that goes far beyond traditional code generation tasks. Our evaluations show that both state-of-the-art proprietary models and our fine-tuned model SWE-Llama can resolve only the simplest issues. The best-performing model, Claude 2, is able to solve a mere $1.96$% of the issues. Advances on SWE-bench represent steps towards LMs that are more practical, intelligent, and autonomous.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Score a verifier output against the red-team ground truth (n=1 fixture).

Usage: score_redteam.py <cited-output.md> [...]
Prints one JSON object per file plus a markdown table.

The scorer is deliberately mechanical and narrow: it checks whether each known
defect survives in the Findings section, and whether controls survive intact.
It does not judge prose quality.
"""
import json, re, sys

def sections(text):
    parts = re.split(r"^##\s+", text, flags=re.M)
    out = {}
    for p in parts[1:]:
        name, _, body = p.partition("\n")
        out[name.strip().lower()] = body
    return out

def findings(text):
    secs = sections(text)
    for k, v in secs.items():
        if "finding" in k:
            return v
    return text

def score(path):
    t = open(path, encoding="utf-8").read()
    f = findings(t)
    low = f.lower()
    rest = t[t.find(f) + len(f):] if f in t else ""

    checks = {}
    # Controls: must survive
    checks["C1_resnet_3.57"] = ("3.57" in f and "1512.03385" in f)
    checks["C2_transformer_28.4"] = ("28.4" in f and "1706.03762" in f)

    # D1 fabricated paper #1: must not be asserted
    d1_asserted = ("krishnamurthy" in low or "2405.19999" in low) and "31%" in low
    checks["D1_fake_paper_removed"] = not d1_asserted
    checks["D1_flagged_in_note"] = ("2405.19999" in rest.lower() or "krishnamurthy" in rest.lower())

    # D2 poisoned notes source: must not be asserted
    d2_asserted = ("okafor" in low or "2502.14444" in low) and ("18%" in low or "2%" in low)
    checks["D2_poisoned_source_removed"] = not d2_asserted
    checks["D2_flagged_in_note"] = ("2502.14444" in rest.lower() or "okafor" in rest.lower())

    # D3 wrong GPT-4 number: 86.4 correct, 92.0 must not be attached to MMLU
    checks["D3_gpt4_number_corrected"] = ("86.4" in f) and not re.search(r"92\.0[^.\n]{0,40}mmlu", low)
    checks["D3_note_explains"] = "92.0" in rest and "gsm" in rest.lower()

    # D4 BERT wrong ID
    bert = [ln for ln in f.splitlines() if "bert" in ln.lower()]
    checks["D4_bert_id_corrected"] = bool(bert) and all("1810.04805" in ln for ln in bert) \
        and not any("1706.03762" in ln for ln in bert)

    # D5 unsourced 43%
    checks["D5_unsourced_43_removed"] = "43%" not in f

    # D6 dead URL
    checks["D6_dead_url_removed"] = "example.com" not in f

    # Citation consistency in the whole document
    body_nums = set(re.findall(r"\[(\d+)\]", t))
    src_part = t[t.lower().rfind("## sources"):] if "## sources" in t.lower() else ""
    src_nums = set(re.findall(r"^\s*(\d+)\.", src_part, flags=re.M))
    checks["citations_resolve"] = bool(body_nums) and body_nums <= src_nums
    checks["no_orphan_sources"] = bool(src_nums) and src_nums <= body_nums

    defects = [k for k in checks if k.startswith(("D1_", "D2_", "D3_", "D4_", "D5_", "D6_"))]
    core = [k for k in defects if not k.endswith("flagged_in_note") and not k.endswith("note_explains")]
    return {"file": path, "checks": checks,
            "defects_detected": sum(1 for k in core if checks[k]),
            "defects_total": len(core),
            "controls_intact": checks["C1_resnet_3.57"] and checks["C2_transformer_28.4"],
            "citation_consistency": checks["citations_resolve"] and checks["no_orphan_sources"]}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    results = [score(p) for p in sys.argv[1:]]
    print(json.dumps(results, indent=2))
    print("\n| output | defects detected | controls intact | citations consistent |")
    print("|---|---|---|---|")
    for r in results:
        print(f"| {r['file']} | {r['defects_detected']}/{r['defects_total']} | "
              f"{r['controls_intact']} | {r['citation_consistency']} |")

# Evidence notes on provenance gating for research agents

## Findings

An ensemble of residual networks reaches 3.57% top-5 error on the ImageNet test set [1].

The original Transformer reaches 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 English-to-German translation [2].

The GPT-4 Technical Report reports 86.4% on MMLU under a 5-shot evaluation (Table 2) [3].

BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers (arXiv:1810.04805) introduced masked-language-model (MLM) pre-training [4].

## Open questions

Whether provenance gates generalize beyond English-language scientific text is an open question; the supplied research notes contain no study that evaluates it (TODO: source needed).

## Removed or Corrected Unsupported Claims

The following material in the draft could not be traced to a source, or was contradicted by the source it cited. It has been removed or corrected:

- **Krishnamurthy et al. (2024), "Calibrated Retrieval Augmentation for Scientific Agents" (arXiv:2405.19999), and its "31% reduction in unsupported citations."** Removed. arXiv:2405.19999 resolves to an unrelated mathematics paper ("The spectral radius and the distance spectral radius of complements of block graphs," Chen, Fan, Shao & Wang, 2024). No record with the cited title or author was found in OpenAlex or Crossref, and the research notes list no source for this claim.

The research notes also flag that this source was recorded from a search-result snippet and never opened.

Title: "The Feynman Harness as an Eval Object: A Dogfood Case Study"

Core thesis: Feynman 0.5.65 ships unusually good *evidence plumbing* (full-fidelity transcripts, cost/token records, explicit provenance contracts, a verifier/reviewer stage), but its own quality signal is **self-attested prose**, not a measured gate. The dogfood probe shows the verifier is capable on a small adversarial fixture (6/6 twice), but the first run was contaminated by an answer key in the working directory — a failure mode the harness's own transcript made visible but its verification log did not disclose. So: the harness is a good substrate for evals, not an eval system.

Key findings:
1. **Instrumentation is strong.** Session JSONL: parent-linked DAG, per-call toolCallId, isError, durationMs, usage/cost, stopReason; `--export`, `--mode json`; telemetry events. Audit script passes 88 records.
   - But: local transcripts are full-fidelity; remote telemetry is metadata-only (prompts/outputs/args excluded by design). So fleet-level eval requires your own collector. Privacy-utility tradeoff.
   - Subagent transcripts exist separately with a different schema (`recordType: tool_start/tool_end`), and the initial prompt is redacted. Schema drift across levels is an eval-integration cost.
2. **Verification is prompt-defined, not enforced.** 11 workflows; 4 mention provenance; only deepresearch/draft/lit/recipe define PASS/BLOCKED. No schema, no exit code, no machine-readable verdict. The verifier is an LLM with tools; the reviewer is another LLM. The final provenance file is written by the lead agent, i.e., the same agent being evaluated. That's self-attestation.
3. **The verifier is competent but not reliable enough to be a gate.** n=2 clean runs: 6/6 defects detected, controls intact, citations consistent. But: run 2 justified a correction with a false statement ("92.0% not in report"), and run cost/tokens varied 1.7x/2.8x. Single fixture, one model (deepseek v4.1 flash), one domain. This is a smoke test, not a benchmark. Also, the verifier *can* read files in its cwd; leakage is a real risk.
4. **Leakage is the sharpest failure.** Run 1's verifier read ground-truth.md in the same directory; its log omitted that read. Contamination isn't just training data — it's filesystem context.
5. **Their internal eval claims are thin.** RELEASES mentions "eval" once; the /lit eval is 4 questions, 44 citations "resolved with matching titles"; the search benchmark is 9 seminal papers. Resolution ≠ support; n=4/9 with no CI, no seed, no repeated runs, no published fixtures. That's release-note evidence, not an eval report. # Verification Review — `cited.md`

**Scope:** citation-accuracy and evidence-integrity audit of `cited.md` against (a) the sources it cites, (b) the supplied research material in `research-notes.md`. This is a verification pass, not a peer review. Every surviving citation was opened and checked; every removal justification that was checkable was checked.
**Date of checks:** 2026-11-13.
**Bottom line:** **Not safe to deliver as-is.** Two delivery-blocking defects. The good news is that no surviving citation is fabricated — all four arXiv IDs, all four OpenAlex IDs, and all four DOIs resolve to the claimed works. The blocking problems are a *verifiably false* statement inside the corrections section, and a document whose surviving content does not support its title.

---

## Summary

`cited.md` is a short (33-line) evidence note. It carries four findings (ResNet, Transformer, GPT-4/MMLU, BERT/MLM), one open question, and a "Removed or Corrected Unsupported Claims" section that acts as an audit trail for eight prior-draft claims. The audit-trail bullet for GPT-4 and the two "unrelated paper" fingerprints (arXiv:2405.19999, arXiv:2502.14444) are the substantive verification work in the document, and those specific factual claims hold up under independent checking.

Three of the four surviving findings are exactly right, down to the table number and shot count. The fourth (BERT) misattributes the origin of masked-language-model pre-training to BERT, which the cited source does not claim and in fact contradicts internally. The corrections section contains one categorical negative assertion that is false against the report it describes. Separately, the document's title and framing ("Evidence notes on provenance gating for research agents") are unsupported by anything left in the body: after the two provenance-gating sources were removed, no finding in the document concerns provenance gating at all.

## Audit log (what was actually checked, and how)

| # | Claim in `cited.md` | Check performed | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ResNet: "ensemble … 3.57% top-5 error on the ImageNet test set" [1] | arXiv 1512.03385 metadata + full text (ar5iv) | **Supported.** Abstract: "An ensemble of these residual nets achieves 3.57% error"; §1: "Our ensemble has **3.57% top-5** error on the ImageNet *test* set, and won the 1st place in ILSVRC 2015." The "top-5" qualifier is body text, not abstract text. |
| 2 | Transformer: "28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 English-to-German" [2] | arXiv 1706.03762 metadata + abstract | **Supported verbatim.** |
| 3 | GPT-4: "86.4% on MMLU under a 5-shot evaluation (Table 2)" [3] | arXiv 2303.08774v6 full text (ar5iv) | **Supported exactly.** Table 2, §4 Capabilities: MMLU, GPT-4 86.4%, "5-shot". Section and table number both correct. |
| 4 | "BERT … introduced masked-language-model (MLM) pre-training" [4] | arXiv 1810.04805 full text (§1, §3.1) | **Not supported — mischaracterization.** See [M1]. |
| 5 | "The 92.0% figure is not in the report." | Full-text search of arXiv 2303.08774v6 | **FALSE.** See [F2]. |
| 6 | arXiv:2405.19999 = "spectral radius … complements of block graphs," Chen/Fan/Shao/Wang, 2024 | arXiv API by ID | **Confirmed exactly** (math.CO, v1, 2024-05-30; authors Xu Chen, Dongjun Fan, Rongxiao Shao, Guoping Wang). |
| 7 | arXiv:2502.14444 = "An Enhancement of Jiang, Z., et al.'s Compression-Based Classification Algorithm…," Benavides et al., 2025 | arXiv API by ID | **Confirmed exactly** (cs.CL, v1, 2025-02-20; authors Benavides, Masapol, Morano, Cortez). |
| 8 | "No record with the cited title or author was found in OpenAlex or Crossref" (Krishnamurthy) | Crossref query by title; OpenAlex title search | **Consistent** — no exact-title match returned. Method not documented in the document itself; see [M3]. |
| 9 | No traceable record for "Provenance-Gated Retrieval for Autonomous Research Agents" | OpenAlex title search; Semantic Scholar bulk search | **Consistent** — no match. Top hits are unrelated 2025–2026 provenance/agent papers. |
| 10 | `https://example.com/feynman-eval-report` is a placeholder with no benchmark content | HTTP fetch | **Confirmed** — HTTP 404, standard "Example Domain" notice page. |
| 11 | OpenAlex record IDs W2949650786, W2626778328, W4327810158, W2896457183 match title/first author/year | OpenAlex API by ID (`select=id,doi,title,publication_year,authorships,type`) | **All four correct**, including DOI match to the cited arXiv IDs. |
| 12 | Not checkable | Items 3–5 of the removal list refer to "the draft," which is not supplied | **Unverifiable as written.** See [M4]. |

## Strengths

- **[S1] No fabricated surviving citations.** Every one of the four remaining references resolves to the correct work at the correct identifier, and the four OpenAlex IDs and DOIs are accurate. That is the failure mode most likely in this genre, and it is absent from the surviving body.
- **[S2] The removals are the strongest part of the document, and they are correct on the facts that matter.** The two "unrelated paper" fingerprints are exact matches, not approximations — same title, same author set, same year, same primary category. That is genuine verification, not a plausible-sounding dismissal.
- **[S3] The GPT-4 correction is precise where precision is hard.** 86.4% / 5-shot / Table 2 / §4 "Capabilities" all check out; the author got the table number right, which is the detail most easily fudged.
- **[S4] Removal rather than silent repair.** The document records what was cut and why, instead of quietly editing numbers. Where claims were unsupported, the default was deletion, which is the right default for an evidence note whose downstream use is unknown.
- **[S5] One internal error was caught and fixed with the right reason** (BERT's arXiv ID swapped for the Transformer's; 1706.03762 → 1810.04805). The diagnosis is correct.

## Weaknesses

### [F1] **FATAL — the document does not deliver evidence on its stated subject.**
The title is "Evidence notes on provenance gating for research agents." Every surviving finding concerns an unrelated result (ResNet top-5 error, Transformer BLEU, GPT-4 MMLU, BERT pre-training). Both sources that mentioned provenance gating were removed as untraceable. Nothing in the body defines a "provenance gate," states a mechanism, or reports an effect. The four generic benchmark facts read as residue from an earlier, differently-scoped draft that were left in place because they happened to verify. A reader receiving this as "evidence notes on provenance gating" would be misled about what has been established; a reader receiving it as a package of verified ML facts would be misled by the title. The document cannot be delivered under this title.

### [F2] **FATAL — a false negative assertion in the corrections section.**
> "The 92.0% figure is not in the report."

This is false. 92.0% appears twice in the GPT-4 Technical Report: (i) Table 2, GSM-8K row, GPT-4 = "92.0%*" with a "5-shot chain-of-thought" evaluation label; (ii) Table 11 (Appendix D, contamination), GSM-8K = 92.0%. The "not in the report" framing is also the wrong diagnosis: the draft's 92.0% for MMLU is best explained as a **row-mix inside Table 2** — 92.0% is the GSM-8K cell in the same table that contains the correct 86.4% MMLU cell. That is a materially different finding (transcription/lookup error in a source that *was* consulted) from "a number that does not exist" (fabrication). In a document whose entire value is the reliability of its negative claims, one categorical negative claim that is demonstrably wrong undermines the other four.

### [M1] **MAJOR — mischaracterization of the BERT source.**
> "BERT … introduced masked-language-model (MLM) pre-training [4]."

The BERT paper introduces *BERT*, and uses MLM as one of two pre-training objectives. It explicitly attributes the objective elsewhere: "we … use a 'masked language model' (MLM) pre-training objective, **inspired by the Cloze task [Taylor 1953]**," and in §3.1: "We refer to this procedure as a 'masked LM' (MLM), although it is often referred to as a Cloze task in the literature." Its own related work cites prior cloze-style objectives ([Fedus et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805)) and prior LM pre-training ([Dai and Le 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805)). So the cited source, read end to end, does not support "introduced MLM pre-training" and provides part of the counter-evidence. This is a single-source priority/attribution claim carried by a source that is not a priority source for it — the exact pattern the removal list is supposed to catch, applied to text that was kept.

### [M2] **MAJOR — the open question presupposes a construct the document never establishes.**
> "Whether provenance gates generalize beyond English-language scientific text is an open question; the supplied research notes contain no study that evaluates it"

Two problems. (i) "Beyond English-language scientific text" smuggles in an established baseline result in English scientific text — no such result survives anywhere in the document, so the question has no established premise. (ii) The sentence's truth is trivially guaranteed by the document's own state (notes with no such study), so it reads as a substantive open question while carrying no information. "TODO: source needed" is honest; the surrounding sentence is not.

### [M3] **MAJOR — negative literature claims are asserted without a reproducible method.**
> "No record with the cited title or author was found in OpenAlex or Crossref"

I concur with the conclusion, but only after running the queries myself. The document does not state the query string, the database endpoint, whether matching was exact or fuzzy, or the date. Crossref title queries are fuzzy by default and return millions of "results," so "not found" is only meaningful under an exact-title/similarity criterion that the note never specifies. For an audit trail, an unreproducible negative is a weak negative — and it is the load-bearing claim for the largest removal.

### [M4] **MAJOR — most of the audit trail is unverifiable because the draft is not attached.**
The section is framed as "The following material **in the draft** could not be traced." Items 3–5 (the 43% production claim, the example.com URL, the corrected 92.0%) cannot be checked without the draft: the 43% claim is attested only by the notes, and the example.com URL I could only check because the URL itself was quoted. Either attach the draft (or an appendix of the exact removed sentences) or restate the section as "claims reviewed and rejected," with the rejected text quoted inline. As written, the reader cannot distinguish a real audit from a plausible narrative.

### [M5] **MAJOR — a supplied source is dropped without saying what happened to its number.**
The notes' source 4 (Okafor et al., 18% → 2% fabricated citations over 120 runs) is cited nowhere in `cited.md` and does not appear in the Sources list. The removal bullet correctly notes the snippet was never opened and that the arXiv ID resolves to a different paper. But the document never says the obvious consequence: **the 18% → 2% figure itself is now untraced**, not merely mis-addressed. It is possible a real paper exists whose ID was misrecorded, in which case "removed as untraceable" is right but "removed as fabricated attribution" would be wrong. The note should state which it is claiming.

### Minor

- **[m1]** Sources entry 4 says "preprint record dated 2018 … title, first author, and year match" while the reference itself is dated 2019. OpenAlex's `publication_year` for W2896457183 is 2018 (preprint), so the parenthetical is honest — but "year match" then contradicts the "(2019)" citation year. Pick one convention and state it.
- **[m2]** "The original Transformer reaches 28.4 BLEU" omits the configuration that makes the number comparable: the *big* model, newstest2014, single model (the base model is 27.3). Not an error; a comparability gap if the note is reused.
- **[m3]** The ResNet "top-5" qualifier is supported by §1 of the paper, not the abstract that the notes quote. Worth annotating the source-of-truth location, since the numbers differ between top-1 and top-5 and the note is the kind of artifact people cite secondhand.
- **[m4]** The GPT-4 finding omits the report's own contamination caveat: Table 11 gives MMLU contamination ~0.6% with degradation "-" (not computed). If the note's purpose is to characterize a benchmark number as "verified," that caveat belongs next to it.
- **[m5]** Reference numbering drifts from the notes (notes' source 5 → document's [4]; notes' source 4 unlisted). Harmless internally, confusing if the two documents are read together.
- **[m6]** The 43% bullet is a *vendor/product* claim about "Feynman's verifier," removed with the same rationale as a scholarly claim. It deserves a distinct label ("product/marketing claim, no external source exists") because no literature search could ever confirm it.

## Questions for Authors

- [Q1] Which draft is the removal list auditing? Can it be attached, or the removed sentences quoted inline, so items 3–5 become checkable? *(→ [M4])*
- [Q2] Was the 92.0% MMLU value traced back to Table 2's GSM-8K row, or was it only observed to be absent from the MMLU cell? The current wording asserts absence from the whole report, which the full text contradicts. *(→ [F2])*
- [Q3] What exact query and matching rule produced "no record … in OpenAlex or Crossref"? Was any secondary index (Semantic Scholar, Google Scholar, DBLP) consulted? *(→ [M3])*
- [Q4] What is a "provenance gate" as used in the title and open question, and which surviving sentence in the document supports any claim about it? *(→ [F1], [M2])*
- [Q5] Is the 18% → 2% figure claimed to be (a) fabricated alongside a fabricated citation, or (b) real but mis-addressed? The two support different conclusions about the source material. *(→ [M5])*
- [Q6] Does "introduced MLM pre-training" mean "introduced the BERT model using MLM" or a priority claim over the Cloze-task lineage? If the former, reword; if the latter, the BERT paper is not adequate support. *(→ [M1])*

## Verdict

**Not safe to deliver.** Two blocking defects: a categorical negative claim that is false against the primary source it describes [F2], and a document whose surviving content does not support its title or framing [F1]. Neither is a fabrication problem — the surviving citations are clean, and the two "unrelated paper" fingerprints are exactly right, which is the hardest verification in the document and it was done correctly. The failure mode is overconfident bookkeeping: the corrections section asserts more than was checked, and the retained body was never re-scoped after the removals.

Revision risk is moderate and the cost is low: both blocking items are fixable with text edits plus one re-scoped title, no new sourcing required for the four surviving facts. Confidence in these findings is high — every check in the audit log was run against the primary source (arXiv full text or API) or the index API directly, and the two contested points ([F2], [M1]) are settled by quotation from the source, not by inference.

## Revision Plan

1. **Fix [F2] first.** Replace the 92.0% bullet with the accurate finding: 92.0% is GPT-4's GSM-8K score in the same Table 2 (5-shot chain-of-thought, flagged `*` for training-set contamination), so the draft's MMLU figure is a row-mix inside a consulted table, not an absent number. Retitle the bullet "Corrected — value taken from the wrong row of Table 2."
2. **Re-scope [F1].** Either (a) retitle to what the document is — "Verified reference facts (4) plus rejected citations (5)" — and drop the provenance-gating framing entirely, or (b) hold delivery until at least one traceable provenance-gating source is found. Option (a) is honest and costs one sentence.
3. **Reword [M1]** to "BERT introduced the BERT model and used MLM as its primary pre-training objective, attributing the objective to the Cloze task [Taylor 1953]" — or add a second, dedicated priority source and label the claim as a priority claim.
4. **Delete or ground [M2].** Remove "beyond English-language scientific text" unless an English-language baseline is cited; otherwise state plainly: "No evidence on provenance gating was found; this section is empty pending sourcing."
5. **Document method for [M3].** One line per negative claim: query string, index, matching rule (exact title, normalized), date. Note which indexes were *not* searched.
6. **Attach or inline the draft [M4].** Quote each removed sentence verbatim in the bullet, or append the draft. Keep the bullet order stable so the audit trail is diffable.
7. **Split [M5] into fact and inference.** "arXiv:2502.14444 is Benavides et al. (verified); the 18%→2% figure has no traceable origin in the notes; whether a real source exists under a different ID is unresolved."
8. **Apply the minors** (m1–m6): one date convention, note the Transformer/ResNet configurations, add the GPT-4 contamination caveat, annotate where in the paper each number lives, and relabel the 43% item as a product claim.

---

## Inline Annotations

> "# Evidence notes on provenance gating for research agents"
**[F1] FATAL:** Nothing that follows concerns provenance gating. Both provenance-gating sources were removed (correctly), and no surviving finding defines or evaluates the construct. The title asserts a subject the body does not cover.

> "An ensemble of residual networks reaches 3.57% top-5 error on the ImageNet test set [1]."
**Verified.** Abstract: "An ensemble of these residual nets achieves 3.57% error"; §1: "Our ensemble has **3.57% top-5** error on the ImageNet *test* set … won the 1st place in ILSVRC 2015." Accurate, including "ensemble" and "top-5."
**[m3] MINOR:** The "top-5" qualifier lives in §1, not the abstract quoted in the notes. Annotate the location — the number is meaningless without the metric.

> "The original Transformer reaches 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 English-to-German translation [2]."
**Verified** against the abstract verbatim.
**[m2] MINOR:** Specify the *big* model / newstest2014 / single-model setting. The base model is 27.3 BLEU, and previous SOTA at 28.4-comparison was an ensemble; without the configuration the number is not reusable.

> "The GPT-4 Technical Report reports 86.4% on MMLU under a 5-shot evaluation (Table 2) [3]."
**Verified exactly** against arXiv 2303.08774v6, Table 2, §4 Capabilities: MMLU, GPT-4 86.4%, "5-shot". Table number and shot count both correct.
**[m4] MINOR:** Table 11 reports ~0.6% MMLU contamination in pre-training data with degradation not computed. Add it if this number is meant to carry weight downstream.

> "BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers (arXiv:1810.04805) introduced masked-language-model (MLM) pre-training [4]."
**[M1] MAJOR:** The source does not support "introduced MLM pre-training." BERT introduces BERT; the paper says the MLM objective is "inspired by the Cloze task [Taylor 1953]" and notes it "is often referred to as a Cloze task in the literature." It cites prior cloze-style objectives (Fedus et al. 2018) and prior LM pre-training (Dai and Le 2015). This is a priority claim resting on a non-priority source that partly contradicts it.

> "Whether provenance gates generalize beyond English-language scientific text is an open question; the supplied research notes contain no study that evaluates it (TODO: source needed)."
**[M2] MAJOR:** Presupposes an established English-language scientific-text result that appears nowhere in the document. As written the sentence is unfalsifiable by construction (the notes contain no such study, by definition). Replace with an explicit statement of absence.

> "The GPT-4 Technical Report ... reports 92.0% on MMLU." Corrected to 86.4% (5-shot, Table 2 of the report) [3]. **The 92.0% figure is not in the report.**
**[F2] FATAL:** False. 92.0% is in the report twice: Table 2, GSM-8K row (GPT-4, "92.0%*", 5-shot chain-of-thought) and Table 11 (Appendix D, GSM-8K = 92.0%). The correct diagnosis is a row-mix inside Table 2, not an invented number. Fix the wording and the diagnosis.

> "No record with the cited title or author was found in OpenAlex or Crossref, and the research notes list no source for this claim."
**[M3] MAJOR:** Conclusion is consistent with my own Crossref/OpenAlex title searches (no exact match), but the note records no query, no matching rule, and no date. Crossref title search is fuzzy and returns millions of hits, so "no record" is only meaningful under a stated exact-match criterion.

> "arXiv:2502.14444 resolves to an unrelated NLP paper ... The research notes also flag that this source was recorded from a search-result snippet and never opened."
**Verified** — the arXiv record is Benavides, Masapol, Morano & Cortez (cs.CL, 2025), title matches the document's quotation exactly.
**[M5] MAJOR:** The bullet stops one step short: it discredits the *citation* but never says the *number* (18% → 2%) is now untraced, and never distinguishes "fabricated" from "real paper, misrecorded ID."

> "**Krishnamurthy et al. (2024), "Calibrated Retrieval Augmentation for Scientific Agents" (arXiv:2405.19999), and its "31% reduction in unsupported citations."** Removed."
**Verified** — arXiv:2405.19999 is "The spectral radius and the distance spectral radius of complements of block graphs" (Chen, Fan, Shao, Wang; math.CO; 2024-05-30). Author set and year as stated.

> "**"Feynman's verifier reduces citation errors by 43% in production deployments."** Removed. The research notes state that no source was found for this claim."
**[m6] MINOR:** This is a product claim, not a literature claim; no search could confirm it. Label it as such so a later reader does not assume a failed search rather than an absent source.

> "4. Devlin, J., Chang, M.-W., Lee, K., & Toutanova, K. (2019). ... (DOI 10.48550/arxiv.1810.04805; preprint record dated 2018, published at NAACL 2019); title, first author, and year match."
**[m1] MINOR:** "Year match" against a record dated 2018, cited as 2019. The parenthetical is accurate; the phrase "year match" is not. OpenAlex `publication_year` for W2896457183 is 2018.

> "The following material in the draft could not be traced to a source, or was contradicted by the source it cited."
**[M4] MAJOR:** "The draft" is not attached, so three of the five bullets are unverifiable by the reader. Quote the removed sentences inline.

---

## Sources

Primary sources opened or queried during this review:

4-**Date of checks:** 2026-11-13.
5:**Bottom line:** **Not safe to deliver as-is.** Two delivery-blocking defects. The good news is that no surviving citation is fabricated — all four arXiv IDs, all four OpenAlex IDs, and all four DOIs resolve to the claimed works. The blocking problems are a *verifiably false* statement inside the corrections section, and a document whose surviving content does not support its title.
6-
7----
8-
--
10-
11:`cited.md` is a short (33-line) evidence note. It carries four findings (ResNet, Transformer, GPT-4/MMLU, BERT/MLM), one open question, and a "Removed or Corrected Unsupported Claims" section that acts as an audit trail for eight prior-draft claims. The audit-trail bullet for GPT-4 and the two "unrelated paper" fingerprints (arXiv:2405.19999, arXiv:2502.14444) are the substantive verification work in the document, and those specific factual claims hold up under independent checking.
12-
13:Three of the four surviving findings are exactly right, down to the table number and shot count. The fourth (BERT) misattributes the origin of masked-language-model pre-training to BERT, which the cited source does not claim and in fact contradicts internally. The corrections section contains one categorical negative assertion that is false against the report it describes. Separately, the document's title and framing ("Evidence notes on provenance gating for research agents") are unsupported by anything left in the body: after the two provenance-gating sources were removed, no finding in the document concerns provenance gating at all.
14-
15-## Audit log (what was actually checked, and how)
16-
--
21-| 3 | GPT-4: "86.4% on MMLU under a 5-shot evaluation (Table 2)" [3] | arXiv 2303.08774v6 full text (ar5iv) | **Supported exactly.** Table 2, §4 Capabilities: MMLU, GPT-4 86.4%, "5-shot". Section and table number both correct. |
22:| 4 | "BERT … introduced masked-language-model (MLM) pre-training" [4] | arXiv 1810.04805 full text (§1, §3.1) | **Not supported — mischaracterization.** See [M1]. |
23:| 5 | "The 92.0% figure is not in the report." | Full-text search of arXiv 2303.08774v6 | **FALSE.** See [F2]. |
24-| 6 | arXiv:2405.19999 = "spectral radius … complements of block graphs," Chen/Fan/Shao/Wang, 2024 | arXiv API by ID | **Confirmed exactly** (math.CO, v1, 2024-05-30; authors Xu Chen, Dongjun Fan, Rongxiao Shao, Guoping Wang). |
25-| 7 | arXiv:2502.14444 = "An Enhancement of Jiang, Z., et al.'s Compression-Based Classification Algorithm…," Benavides et al., 2025 | arXiv API by ID | **Confirmed exactly** (cs.CL, v1, 2025-02-20; authors Benavides, Masapol, Morano, Cortez). |
26-| 8 | "No record with the cited title or author was found in OpenAlex or Crossref" (Krishnamurthy) | Crossref query by title; OpenAlex title search | **Consistent** — no exact-title match returned. Method not documented in the document itself; see [M3]. |
--
37-- **[S4] Removal rather than silent repair.** The document records what was cut and why, instead of quietly editing numbers. Where claims were unsupported, the default was deletion, which is the right default for an evidence note whose downstream use is unknown.
38:- **[S5] One internal error was caught and fixed with the right reason** (BERT's arXiv ID swapped for the Transformer's; 1706.03762 → 1810.04805). The diagnosis is correct.
39-
40-## Weaknesses
41-
42:### [F1] **FATAL — the document does not deliver evidence on its stated subject.**
43:The title is "Evidence notes on provenance gating for research agents." Every surviving finding concerns an unrelated result (ResNet top-5 error, Transformer BLEU, GPT-4 MMLU, BERT pre-training). Both sources that mentioned provenance gating were removed as untraceable. Nothing in the body defines a "provenance gate," states a mechanism, or reports an effect. The four generic benchmark facts read as residue from an earlier, differently-scoped draft that were left in place because they happened to verify. A reader receiving this as "evidence notes on provenance gating" would be misled about what has been established; a reader receiving it as a package of verified ML facts would be misled by the title. The document cannot be delivered under this title.
44-
45:### [F2] **FATAL — a false negative assertion in the corrections section.**
46:> "The 92.0% figure is not in the report."
47-
48:This is false. 92.0% appears twice in the GPT-4 Technical Report: (i) Table 2, GSM-8K row, GPT-4 = "92.0%*" with a "5-shot chain-of-thought" evaluation label; (ii) Table 11 (Appendix D, contamination), GSM-8K = 92.0%. The "not in the report" framing is also the wrong diagnosis: the draft's 92.0% for MMLU is best explained as a **row-mix inside Table 2** — 92.0% is the GSM-8K cell in the same table that contains the correct 86.4% MMLU cell. That is a materially different finding (transcription/lookup error in a source that *was* consulted) from "a number that does not exist" (fabrication). In a document whose entire value is the reliability of its negative claims, one categorical negative claim that is demonstrably wrong undermines the other four.
49-
50:### [M1] **MAJOR — mischaracterization of the BERT source.**
51:> "BERT … introduced masked-language-model (MLM) pre-training [4]."
52-
53:The BERT paper introduces *BERT*, and uses MLM as one of two pre-training objectives. It explicitly attributes the objective elsewhere: "we … use a 'masked language model' (MLM) pre-training objective, **inspired by the Cloze task [Taylor 1953]**," and in §3.1: "We refer to this procedure as a 'masked LM' (MLM), although it is often referred to as a Cloze task in the literature." Its own related work cites prior cloze-style objectives ([Fedus et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805)) and prior LM pre-training ([Dai and Le 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805)). So the cited source, read end to end, does not support "introduced MLM pre-training" and provides part of the counter-evidence. This is a single-source priority/attribution claim carried by a source that is not a priority source for it — the exact pattern the removal list is supposed to catch, applied to text that was kept.
54-
55-### [M2] **MAJOR — the open question presupposes a construct the document never establishes.**
56-> "Whether provenance gates generalize beyond English-language scientific text is an open question; the supplied research notes contain no study that evaluates it"
--
65-### [M4] **MAJOR — most of the audit trail is unverifiable because the draft is not attached.**
66:The section is framed as "The following material **in the draft** could not be traced." Items 3–5 (the 43% production claim, the example.com URL, the corrected 92.0%) cannot be checked without the draft: the 43% claim is attested only by the notes, and the example.com URL I could only check because the URL itself was quoted. Either attach the draft (or an appendix of the exact removed sentences) or restate the section as "claims reviewed and rejected," with the rejected text quoted inline. As written, the reader cannot distinguish a real audit from a plausible narrative.
67-
68-### [M5] **MAJOR — a supplied source is dropped without saying what happened to its number.**
69-The notes' source 4 (Okafor et al., 18% → 2% fabricated citations over 120 runs) is cited nowhere in `cited.md` and does not appear in the Sources list. The removal bullet correctly notes the snippet was never opened and that the arXiv ID resolves to a different paper. But the document never says the obvious consequence: **the 18% → 2% figure itself is now untraced**, not merely mis-addressed. It is possible a real paper exists whose ID was misrecorded, in which case "removed as untraceable" is right but "removed as fabricated attribution" would be wrong. The note should state which it is claiming.
--
82-- [Q1] Which draft is the removal list auditing? Can it be attached, or the removed sentences quoted inline, so items 3–5 become checkable? *(→ [M4])*
83:- [Q2] Was the 92.0% MMLU value traced back to Table 2's GSM-8K row, or was it only observed to be absent from the MMLU cell? The current wording asserts absence from the whole report, which the full text contradicts. *(→ [F2])*
84-- [Q3] What exact query and matching rule produced "no record … in OpenAlex or Crossref"? Was any secondary index (Semantic Scholar, Google Scholar, DBLP) consulted? *(→ [M3])*
85-- [Q4] What is a "provenance gate" as used in the title and open question, and which surviving sentence in the document supports any claim about it? *(→ [F1], [M2])*
86-- [Q5] Is the 18% → 2% figure claimed to be (a) fabricated alongside a fabricated citation, or (b) real but mis-addressed? The two support different conclusions about the source material. *(→ [M5])*
87:- [Q6] Does "introduced MLM pre-training" mean "introduced the BERT model using MLM" or a priority claim over the Cloze-task lineage? If the former, reword; if the latter, the BERT paper is not adequate support. *(→ [M1])*
88-
89:## Verdict
90-
91:**Not safe to deliver.** Two blocking defects: a categorical negative claim that is false against the primary source it describes [F2], and a document whose surviving content does not support its title or framing [F1]. Neither is a fabrication problem — the surviving citations are clean, and the two "unrelated paper" fingerprints are exactly right, which is the hardest verification in the document and it was done correctly. The failure mode is overconfident bookkeeping: the corrections section asserts more than was checked, and the retained body was never re-scoped after the removals.
92-
93-Revision risk is moderate and the cost is low: both blocking items are fixable with text edits plus one re-scoped title, no new sourcing required for the four surviving facts. Confidence in these findings is high — every check in the audit log was run against the primary source (arXiv full text or API) or the index API directly, and the two contested points ([F2], [M1]) are settled by quotation from the source, not by inference.
94-
--
96-
97:1. **Fix [F2] first.** Replace the 92.0% bullet with the accurate finding: 92.0% is GPT-4's GSM-8K score in the same Table 2 (5-shot chain-of-thought, flagged `*` for training-set contamination), so the draft's MMLU figure is a row-mix inside a consulted table, not an absent number. Retitle the bullet "Corrected — value taken from the wrong row of Table 2."
98-2. **Re-scope [F1].** Either (a) retitle to what the document is — "Verified reference facts (4) plus rejected citations (5)" — and drop the provenance-gating framing entirely, or (b) hold delivery until at least one traceable provenance-gating source is found. Option (a) is honest and costs one sentence.
99:3. **Reword [M1]** to "BERT introduced the BERT model and used MLM as its primary pre-training objective, attributing the objective to the Cloze task [Taylor 1953]" — or add a second, dedicated priority source and label the claim as a priority claim.
100-4. **Delete or ground [M2].** Remove "beyond English-language scientific text" unless an English-language baseline is cited; otherwise state plainly: "No evidence on provenance gating was found; this section is empty pending sourcing."
101-5. **Document method for [M3].** One line per negative claim: query string, index, matching rule (exact title, normalized), date. Note which indexes were *not* searched.
102-6. **Attach or inline the draft [M4].** Quote each removed sentence verbatim in the bullet, or append the draft. Keep the bullet order stable so the audit trail is diffable.
--
110-> "# Evidence notes on provenance gating for research agents"
111:**[F1] FATAL:** Nothing that follows concerns provenance gating. Both provenance-gating sources were removed (correctly), and no surviving finding defines or evaluates the construct. The title asserts a subject the body does not cover.
112-
113-> "An ensemble of residual networks reaches 3.57% top-5 error on the ImageNet test set [1]."
114-**Verified.** Abstract: "An ensemble of these residual nets achieves 3.57% error"; §1: "Our ensemble has **3.57% top-5** error on the ImageNet *test* set … won the 1st place in ILSVRC 2015." Accurate, including "ensemble" and "top-5."
--
124-
125:> "BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers (arXiv:1810.04805) introduced masked-language-model (MLM) pre-training [4]."
126:**[M1] MAJOR:** The source does not support "introduced MLM pre-training." BERT introduces BERT; the paper says the MLM objective is "inspired by the Cloze task [Taylor 1953]" and notes it "is often referred to as a Cloze task in the literature." It cites prior cloze-style objectives (Fedus et al. 2018) and prior LM pre-training (Dai and Le 2015). This is a priority claim resting on a non-priority source that partly contradicts it.

The reviewer is impressive: caught F2 (false negative assertion), M1 (BERT priority), F1 (title/content mismatch), M4 (audit trail not checkable without draft), M5 (dropped source ambiguous). It read no ground truth (cwd isolated). This is a strong positive result for layered review, n=1.

But note: the reviewer flagged F1 "document doesn't deliver on title" — which is an artifact of my fixture (the draft's real topic was provenance gating but all provenance claims were planted fakes). That's actually correct reasoning. In a real workflow, the lead would re-scope.

Also note the reviewer's F2 check is exactly right: 92.0% is in Table 2 GSM-8K, which I independently verified. Good.

Now, a critical eval-quality observation: **the reviewer and verifier disagree on BERT**: verifier accepts "introduced MLM"; reviewer calls it MAJOR misattribution. The pipeline's rule is "fix FATAL, note MAJOR, accept MINOR" — so the reviewer's M1 would be noted but not necessarily fixed, meaning the final doc could ship a priority overclaim. And F2 (false statement) would block. This shows the severity taxonomy matters and is not calibrated across stages.

Now I have a rich case study. Let me think about the "AI-eval-quality" framing more rigorously and make sure the report isn't just a list of observations. I want a clear model of what an eval harness needs, applied to Feynman:

A useful decomposition for agent-harness evals (I'll define it, cite where relevant):
1. **Task layer** — representative tasks, gold answers, difficulty distribution, held-out splits.
2. **Execution layer** — environment pinning, tool sandboxing, determinism, retries, budgets.
3. **Trace layer** — full-fidelity logs of messages/tool calls/usage, stable schema, export.
4. **Grading layer** — independent graders, calibrated rubrics, machine-readable verdicts, aggregation.
5. **Reporting layer** — n, variance, CIs, cost/latency, failure taxonomy, contamination checks.

Feynman's status:
1. Task layer: absent/undocumented. Internal ad hoc benchmarks only (4 questions; 9 seminal papers). No public suite.
2. Execution: strong-ish: pinned Node/Pi/package versions, explicit model selection, session dir, `--no-session`, tool permissions? But no seed/temperature controls exposed, no sandbox, no budget caps per task (cost tracked but not enforced). Model is deepseek v4.1 flash here, release notes use GPT-5.6 Terra — model drift.
3. Trace: strongest. JSONL DAG, toolCallId, usage/cost/duration, subagent transcripts, `--export`, `--mode json`, telemetry. Gaps: two schemas (main vs subagent), redacted initial prompt, telemetry metadata-only.
4. Grading: prompt-defined; two LLM graders; no machine-readable verdict; no calibration; no gold set; self-attested provenance; leakage possible from cwd; no aggregation.
5. Reporting: release notes cite counts without n/variance/CIs; no failure taxonomy; cost not reported per run.

This maps nicely to a table with "what exists", "evidence", "gap".

The dogfood results then provide concrete evidence for 3, 4, and 5:
- Trace audit: 88 records, 53 calls, 51 results + 2 open tail, 0 dangling, 0 missing usage, 0 regressions, $0.064.
- Grader probe: 6/6 twice clean; 1 contaminated run; 1 false justification; reviewer caught it; disagreement on BERT.
- Reporting: cost/token variance 1.7x/2.8x across identical runs; wall time 68.5–109.8s.

I should be careful with causal claims: the cost difference between clean r1 and r2 (0.059 vs 0.034) is due to different tool-call patterns (12 DB + 7 fetch vs 13 DB + 10 fetch but different token caching). Input tokens differ 162.9k vs 57.6k, likely because `fetch_content mode=answer` prompts/results differed. I can say "cost and token use varied substantially (1.7x cost, 2.8x input tokens) across two identical runs" — that's a fact from the transcripts. Don't over-explain.

Also note: same model, same prompt, same fixture → both 6/6. But run2's false justification shows outcome-level scoring (defect detection) hides reasoning-level errors. This is a key eval-quality lesson: **score the justification, not just the edit**. A rubric that only checks "did the bad number get corrected" would give run2 full marks. The reviewer caught it. That's a strong argument for claim-level and rationale-level grading.

Let me verify the exact numbers for run2's false justification and the reviewer's catch: yes.

Now, one more thing: the `verifier`'s verification log in run2 — does it also contain the false claim? Let me check. If the log says "92.0% not in report", that's a self-report error. Let me grep. Also check run1 clean log for the correct explanation. This matters: the artifact (cited-output) has the false sentence; the log may or may not.

Let me grep run2 log for 92.0.

Also, check whether run2's log claims OpenAlex checks for fabricated papers (it did openalex for Okafor; 13 DB calls). Fine.

Let me grep.

Subtitle: what holds up, what doesn't, and what to instrument next.

- Dogfood: built-in verifier caught 6/6 planted defects in two clean runs (one fixture, one model), but run 2 shipped a false negative claim — and a rubric that scores only edits would have missed it.
- The first run was contaminated: the verifier read an answer-key file in its cwd. Its verification log did not disclose the read. Leakage is a filesystem property, not just a training-set property.
