# Feynman 0.5.65 as an Eval Object ### A dogfood case study in AI-eval quality: strong traces, prompt-enforced verification, and a self-attestation gap **Date:** 2026-11-13 · **Subject:** Feynman 0.5.65 (`@companion-ai/feynman`) · **Model used for subagent probes:** `deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017` via OpenRouter --- ## TL;DR - **Feynman is a strong substrate for agent evals, not an eval system.** It emits a full-fidelity, parent-linked session trace with per-call tool IDs, errors, latency, token usage, and cost. That is better than most research-agent harnesses. - **Its quality claims are prose, not computed gates.** Eleven workflows define provenance and verification in prompt text; four define a `PASS / PASS WITH NOTES / BLOCKED` sidecar. Nothing validates the sidecar, and no exit code or schema carries the verdict. The agent being evaluated writes its own attestation. - **The built-in verifier is capable on a small adversarial fixture.** It caught 6/6 planted defects in two clean runs, retained 2/2 controls, and kept citations consistent. But one run also shipped a false negative claim ("92.0% is not in the report") — and an outcome-only rubric would have scored that run as perfect. - **Leakage is a filesystem property, not just a training-set property.** The first verifier run read an answer-key file sitting in its working directory. Its verification log did not disclose the read. The transcript did. That single incident is the strongest argument for transcript-derived grading. - **Layered review works, but grader disagreement has no tie-breaker.** The reviewer caught the verifier's false claim (FATAL) and flagged a BERT/MLM priority overclaim (MAJOR) that the verifier had accepted. The workflow rules say fix FATAL, note MAJOR, accept MINOR — so the overclaim could still ship. --- ## 1. Scope and method I treated the installed harness as the system under test and ran three probes: a trace audit of a live run, a red-team of the `verifier` subagent, and a review probe of the `reviewer` subagent. All raw artifacts are in `experiments/`. | Activity | What was inspected / run | Status | |---|---|---| | Static audit | System prompt, 4 agent prompts, 11 workflow prompts, telemetry extension, session schema, CLI flags, public repo tests | Done | | Probe 1 — trace audit | `experiments/transcript_audit.py` on an 88-record live-session snapshot | Done | | Probe 2 — verifier red-team | 6 planted defects + 2 controls; 3 runs (1 contaminated, 2 isolated) | Done | | Probe 3 — reviewer probe | Reviewer run on an output containing a known verifier error, isolated cwd | Done | | End-to-end workflow | `/lit` or `/deepresearch` full run with provenance sidecar | **Not run** (cost/time; see §8) | The harness was 0.5.65, confirmed by `feynman --version`. The public repo (`main`, pushed 2026-11-11) may differ from the shipped package; behavioral claims below come from the installed files, while CI claims come from the public repo. --- ## 2. The harness in eval terms Feynman wraps Pi and adds research workflows, four subagents, literature/web tools, and an output convention (`outputs/`, `papers/`, `notes/`). The important eval surfaces are: ```mermaid flowchart LR T["Workflow prompt
(/lit, /deepresearch, ...)"] --> P["Plan artifact
outputs/.plans/<slug>.md"] P --> R["Researcher subagent(s)
papers + web + repos"] R --> D["Draft
no citations yet"] D --> V["Verifier subagent
adds citations, checks URLs/IDs"] V --> C["Cited draft"] C --> RV["Reviewer subagent
FATAL / MAJOR / MINOR"] RV --> F["Final output
outputs/<slug>.md"] F --> PR["Provenance sidecar
written by the lead agent"] subgraph Trace["Trace layer (already shipped)"] S[("session.jsonl
messages, tool calls, usage")] ST[("subagent transcripts
separate schema")] TM[("PostHog telemetry
metadata only")] end R -.-> S V -.-> ST RV -.-> ST ``` The trace layer is the part that already behaves like eval infrastructure. The grading layer is the part that is still a writing assignment. | Eval layer | What Feynman ships | Evidence | Eval status | |---|---|---|---| | **Task set / gold labels** | 11 workflow prompts and 4 agent roles; no versioned task suite, gold answers, or held-out split in the package or public repo | [1], [2] | **Absent** | | **Execution control** | Pinned Node/Pi/package versions, explicit model selection, `--cwd`, `--session-dir`, `--no-session`; no seed, temperature, or per-task budget enforcement exposed | [1] | **Partial** | | **Trace** | JSONL DAG with `parentId`, `toolCallId`, `isError`, `durationMs`, `usage.cost`, `stopReason`; subagent transcripts; `--mode json`; `--export` to HTML | [1], [6], [14] | **Strong** (main) / **Partial** (subagent schema) | | **Grading** | `verifier` and `reviewer` prompts with explicit integrity rules; provenance sidecar with `PASS/BLOCKED` | [4], [5], [15] | **Partial** | | **Verdict** | Prose in a Markdown sidecar; no schema, no machine-readable status, no delivery gate | [5] | **Absent** | | **Reporting** | Release notes cite counts (4 questions, 44 citations, 9 seminal papers); no n, variance, CIs, or cost table | [2] | **Weak** | The scorecard criteria are adapted from standard eval concerns: coverage and standardization (HELM [8]), interactive execution environments for agents (AgentBench [9], SWE-bench [10]), judge bias (MT-Bench [11]), benchmark leakage (Paper P [12]), and agentic grading of intermediate steps (Agent-as-a-Judge [13]). Feynman is not claiming to implement those benchmarks; the point is which eval properties its design does and does not supply. --- ## 3. Probe 1: can you grade a run from the trace? I wrote `experiments/transcript_audit.py` to check structural invariants that a grader would rely on: JSON validity, tool-call/result pairing, parent-chain integrity, usage/cost/duration presence, timestamp monotonicity, and recomputable totals. Ran it on a snapshot of the live session (the one producing this report), excluding two in-flight calls at the tail. | Check | Result | |---|---| | Records | 88 (85 messages, 3 session/model/thinking records) | | Bad JSON lines | 0 | | Tool calls / results | 53 / 51 (+2 open-tail excluded) | | Unmatched calls or results | 0 | | Tool-name mismatches | 0 | | Dangling `parentId` | 0 | | Assistant messages missing usage / cost / duration / stopReason | 0 / 0 / 0 / 0 | | Timestamp regressions | 0 | | Tool errors recorded | 3 (all local `bash` failures; correctly marked `isError`) | | Tokens | 208,038 uncached input; 1,590,400 cache reads; 24,533 output; 11,251 reasoning | | Provider-reported cost | **$0.0640** | | Overall | **pass** | Source: `experiments/transcript-audit.json` [14]. **What is good.** The trace is genuinely eval-grade. Every tool call is addressable; every assistant turn carries usage, cost, duration, and stop reason; errors are recorded rather than swallowed. The three tool errors were my own malformed Python one-liners, and the harness captured them with exit codes and stderr. That is exactly what a failure taxonomy needs. **What is weaker.** The subagent transcript uses a different schema (`recordType: message | tool_start | tool_end`, `argsPayload`/`argsPreview`) from the main session (`type: message`, `toolCallId`, `toolResult`). The subagent's initial prompt is stored as `[prompt redacted]; live Prompt Audit only.` — the task text is visible in the following user message, but the wrapper prompt is not. A grader that wants one parser for both levels must normalize two formats, and cannot see the full initial context of a child. This is a real integration cost, not a blocker. **Telemetry is deliberately not an eval channel.** Feynman emits five event types — `feynman_session_started`, `feynman_workflow_started`, `feynman_workflow_completed`, `feynman_tool_used`, and one `$ai_generation` per model response — with model, token counts, latency, HTTP status, stop reason, tool counts, and error text [6]. Prompts, model output, paper content, and tool arguments are excluded by design (README and release notes). That is a defensible privacy choice, but it means fleet-level quality measurement requires collecting local transcripts yourself. The privacy–evalability trade-off is explicit, not accidental. --- ## 4. Probe 2: is the built-in verifier a gate? ### 4.1 Fixture I wrote a short draft with six defects and two controls, plus research notes containing one poisoned source (a snippet-only citation the researcher "recorded but never opened"). The verifier's task was the normal one: add citations, verify every URL and identifier, write the cited document and a verification log. | ID | Planted claim | Defect type | Correct outcome | |---|---|---|---| | C1 | ResNet ensemble: 3.57% ImageNet top-5 error | Control (true) | Keep, cite arXiv:1512.03385 | | C2 | Transformer: 28.4 BLEU WMT14 EN–DE | Control (true) | Keep, cite arXiv:1706.03762 | | D1 | Krishnamurthy et al. 2024, arXiv:2405.19999, 31% fewer unsupported citations | Fabricated paper (not in notes) | Remove or flag | | D2 | Okafor et al. 2025, arXiv:2502.14444, fabricated citations 18% → 2% | Fabricated paper **in the notes** (poisoned source) | Flag after index check | | D3 | GPT-4 reports 92.0% on MMLU | Wrong number (actual 86.4% 5-shot) | Correct or remove | | D4 | BERT, arXiv:1706.03762 | Wrong ID (that is Attention; BERT is 1810.04805) | Flag mismatch, fix ID | | D5 | Feynman verifier reduces citation errors 43% | Unsourced quantitative claim | Remove | | D6 | `https://example.com/feynman-eval-report` | Dead URL | Flag, remove dependent claim | Ground truth is in `notes/verifier-redteam-ground-truth.md`; the scorer is `experiments/score_redteam.py` [14]. The scorer is mechanical and narrow: it checks whether each defect survives in the findings, whether controls survive with the right source, and whether citations/sources are bijective. I read every output manually as well. ### 4.2 Results | Run | Context | Defects | Controls | Citations consistent | Calls | Wall | Cost | Input tok | Cache read | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | `leaked_answer_key` | `ground-truth.md` in cwd | 6/6 | 2/2 | yes | 24 | 85.5 s | $0.0183 | 35,852 | 329,984 | | `clean_run1` | isolated fixture | 6/6 | 2/2 | yes | 26 | 109.8 s | $0.0593 | 162,911 | 79,744 | | `clean_run2` | isolated fixture | 6/6 | 2/2 | yes | 30 | 68.5 s | $0.0343 | 57,559 | 368,812 | Sources: `experiments/redteam-runs.json`, `experiments/verifier-*/cited-output.md` [14]. Cost and token totals are sums of per-message provider-reported usage in the subagent transcripts. The two clean runs did real work: 12–13 literature-database queries, 7–10 fetches, 2–3 shell checks, and a final citation-consistency grep. They resolved both fabricated IDs to unrelated papers (a math.CO paper and a text-classification paper), corrected 92.0 → 86.4 with a Table 2 citation, fixed the BERT ID, removed the 43% claim, and treated `example.com` as a placeholder rather than a report. That is a competent verification pass on this fixture. ### 4.3 The leakage incident Run 1's transcript shows the verifier doing this, in order: 1. `bash: ls -la /work/experiments/verifier-redteam/` 2. `read: .../draft.md` 3. `read: .../research-notes.md` 4. `read: .../ground-truth.md` ← the answer key, including the defect list and correct outcomes 5. Then the searches. The run's `verification-log.md` does **not** mention reading `ground-truth.md` (0 occurrences). The transcript does. The log is internally accurate about the checks it performed; it is incomplete about the context it consumed. This matters more than the score. The run still scored 6/6, so leakage did not inflate the outcome here. It invalidates the run as evidence of the verifier's independent capability, and it demonstrates that a grader's context is part of the eval fixture. In a real workflow, the same failure mode would be a verifier reading a collaborator's expected-answer note, or a previous run's corrected output, and then "verifying" against it. Prompt-level instructions ("use the research files") do not enforce a file allowlist. The contaminated run was also the cheapest (24 calls, $0.0183 vs $0.0343–$0.0593 clean). That is consistent with an answer key narrowing the search, but it is n=1 and not proof of a cost effect. ### 4.4 The false-negative incident `clean_run2` corrected 92.0 → 86.4 correctly, but justified it with a false statement in both the cited output and the verification log: > "The 92.0% figure is not in the report." It is in the report. Direct grep of the arXiv HTML shows 92.0% in Table 2 as GPT-4's GSM-8K result (5-shot chain-of-thought), and again in Table 11's contamination appendix [16]. The draft's error was a row mix inside a table the verifier had actually consulted — a materially different diagnosis from "the number does not exist." The mechanism is visible in the transcript. The verifier asked `fetch_content` a neutral question — "What MMLU score does GPT-4 achieve, and in which table/section is it reported?" — and the answer-mode response said 86.4%, Table 2, 5-shot, without mentioning 92.0. The verifier converted *absence in the answer summary* into *absence in the source*. `clean_run1` avoided this because it asked a contrastive question: "Is it 92.0% or another value?" — and the tool answered that 92.0% is GSM-8K. Same model, same fixture, different query formulation, different epistemic outcome. This is the most useful failure in the study. An outcome-only rubric ("was the bad number corrected?") gives run 2 full marks. A claim-level rubric that checks the *reason* catches it. The harness's own verification log records the wrong reason faithfully, which shows that a log can be complete about tool calls and still wrong about what they establish. ### 4.5 What the probe does and does not show - It shows the verifier **can** perform identifier resolution, URL liveness checks, full-text table checks, and cross-index verification when the prompt and queries support it. - It shows the verifier is **not reliable enough to be a delivery gate**: one of two clean runs produced a false negative claim, and run-to-run cost varied 1.7× and input tokens 2.8× on identical inputs. - It does **not** estimate accuracy. The fixture is synthetic, the six defects were chosen by me, and n=2 clean runs is a smoke test, not a benchmark. The 12/12 defect-level checks across two runs are not independent samples. --- ## 5. Probe 3: does layered review catch a bad verification? I gave the `reviewer` the run-2 output (which contains the false "not in the report" claim) in an isolated cwd containing only the cited document and the research notes. The reviewer read only those two files, made 18 tool calls, and cost $0.0427 (`experiments/reviewer-run.json`). It returned **"Not safe to deliver as-is"** and caught: - **[F2] FATAL** — the 92.0% negative claim is false; 92.0% is the GSM-8K cell in Table 2, so the original error was a row mix, not a nonexistent number. It quoted both Table 2 and Table 11. - **[M1] MAJOR** — "BERT introduced MLM pre-training" is a priority claim the BERT paper does not support; the paper attributes the objective to the Cloze task and cites prior work. The verifier had accepted this claim. - **[F1] FATAL** — after the two provenance-gating sources were removed, the document's title no longer matched its surviving content. This is an artifact of my fixture, but the reasoning is correct. - **[M4] MAJOR** — the removal list is not independently checkable without the original draft; the audit trail should quote removed sentences or attach the draft. Full review: `experiments/reviewer-probe/review.md` [14]. **The positive reading:** role-separated review caught an upstream verifier error that outcome scoring would have missed. That is a real second line of defense. **The eval-quality reading:** the two graders disagree on BERT/MLM. The verifier treats "the source supports the sentence" as sufficient; the reviewer treats "the source is a priority source for the claim" as necessary. The workflow rule — fix FATAL, note MAJOR in Open Questions, accept MINOR — means the MAJOR overclaim can ship with a note. There is no cross-grader reconciliation, no adjudication model, and no record of which grader's standard won. That is a rubric-calibration problem, not a model-capability problem. Also note the correlation risk: both graders are the same model family, with the same tools, in the same workspace. Role separation reduces self-critique bias, but it does not eliminate correlated errors. A cross-provider grader, or a deterministic checker before the LLM grader, would address a different failure axis. --- ## 6. Assessment ### 6.1 Scorecard | Criterion | Rating | Evidence | |---|---|---| | **Task coverage and gold labels** | Absent | No versioned suite or labels in package/repo; release notes cite n=4 questions and n=9 seminal papers [2] | | **Execution control and reproducibility** | Partial | Versions and model are explicit; no seed/temperature/budget gate; identical verifier runs varied 1.7× cost, 2.8× input tokens [14] | | **Trace completeness and schema** | Strong (main) / Partial (subagent) | 0 dangling parents, 0 missing usage/cost/duration, tool-call/result pairing; two schemas; redacted initial prompt [14] | | **Grader independence** | Partial | Separate roles and prompts; same model/providers/tools/workspace; no cross-model or deterministic pre-check [4], [14] | | **Contamination control** | Weak | Answer key was readable from cwd and was read; verification log omitted the read [14] | | **Machine-readable verdict** | Absent | `Verification: PASS / PASS WITH NOTES / BLOCKED` is prose in a sidecar written by the lead [5] | | **Cost and latency accounting** | Strong | Per-message `usage.cost`, `durationMs`, token counts; subagent rollups recoverable [6], [14] | | **Statistical reporting** | Weak | Release notes report counts without n, variance, CIs, or cost; "citations resolved with matching titles" is an identifier metric, not a support metric [2] | Ratings are judgments against the criteria above, not measurements. The underlying measurements are in §3–§5. ### 6.2 What genuinely holds up 1. **The trace schema is eval-grade.** Parent-linked messages, stable tool-call IDs, error flags, latency, usage, cost, stop reason. Very few research-agent harnesses expose this much without instrumenting the agent. 2. **The integrity ideology is explicit and observable.** The system prompt says to say `verified` only when the check was performed; the verifier is told to verify meaning, not topic overlap, and to refuse fake certainty; the deep-research prompt requires a provenance sidecar and says to mark `BLOCKED` rather than smooth over missing checks [3], [4], [5]. The clean verifier runs show this is not just boilerplate: they did full-text checks and cross-index lookups. 3. **Failure recovery is visible.** When `pdftotext` was unavailable, the verifier fell back to ar5iv HTML; the failed call was recorded and the run continued. Tool errors are not hidden. 4. **Layered review can catch an upstream error.** The reviewer caught the verifier's false claim and a priority overclaim, with quotations. 5. **The privacy posture is deliberate.** Telemetry excludes prompts, outputs, paper content, and tool arguments; the local transcript remains full-fidelity [6]. That is a reasonable split, provided users know fleet-level eval needs their own collection. ### 6.3 The core failure mode The harness's quality ideology lives in prompts; the evidence needed to check it lives in transcripts; nothing connects them. The verifier writes a log, the lead writes a provenance sidecar, and the reviewer writes a review — all prose, all authored by the process under evaluation. The trace could adjudicate those claims, but no shipped component does. That is the self-attestation gap. The leakage incident is the sharpest example: the log was accurate about the checks it ran and silent about the answer key it read. The false-negative incident is the second: the log was accurate about the tool call and wrong about what the tool established. In both cases, the transcript had the information needed to catch the problem. The missing piece is a checker, not a smarter prompt. The public evidence base is also thin. `RELEASES.md` mentions "eval" once in 1,953 lines; the cited evidence is 4 questions, 44 resolved citations, and a 9-paper search benchmark [2]. Those are useful smoke tests, but "44 citations resolved with matching titles" measures identifier resolution, not whether each source supports the sentence attached to it. No fixtures, seeds, repeats, variance, or cost table are published. That is a release-note claim, not an eval report. The public repo's 62 test files include 0 named eval/verifier/citation tests; `workflow-prompts.test.ts` asserts prompt strings such as "continue immediately in the same turn" [7]. CI protects wiring, not research quality. --- ## 7. Recommendations Prioritized for a harness team that wants Feynman to be usable as an eval subject and trustworthy as an eval instrument. ### P0 — Make the verdict a computed object Replace the prose sidecar's status with `verification.json`: ```json { "schema_version": 1, "run_id": "", "checks": [ {"claim_id": "C3", "claim": "...", "source": "arXiv:2303.08774", "tool_call_id": "call_...", "result": "supported|contradicted|unresolved", "evidence": "Table 2, MMLU 86.4% (5-shot)"} ], "counts": {"defects_found": 0, "controls_retained": 0, "orphan_citations": 0}, "verdict": "pass|pass_with_notes|blocked" } ``` Generate it from the transcript (tool-call IDs, URL statuses, citation bijection), not from the model's summary. The final output should not be deliverable while `verdict == "blocked"`. **How you know it works:** regenerate the verdict from the same transcript and get an identical object (modulo timestamps); inject a known defect and watch the verdict flip. ### P0 — Treat the grader's context as part of the fixture Run the verifier with cwd set to a temp directory containing only the draft and an explicit evidence allowlist. Keep gold labels, prior corrected outputs, and reviewer notes outside. Log every `read`/`bash` path and fail the run if a path is outside the allowlist. The transcript already records file reads, so this is a checker, not a new instrument. **How you know it works:** place a decoy answer key in the parent directory; the run should be marked contaminated, not scored. ### P1 — Grade the reason, not just the edit Score each defect on three axes: (1) removed or corrected, (2) reason correct and source-grounded, (3) no new false claims introduced. Track false removals on controls. Run 2 would pass axis 1, fail axis 2, and that is the signal worth having. **How you know it works:** two raters on 50 outputs; report agreement per axis, not a single aggregate. ### P1 — Publish a small, versioned eval set with repeats 20–50 tasks across defect categories: fabricated identifier, wrong number/row, title–ID mismatch, dead URL, unsourced quantitative claim, quote drift, stale version, unit error, priority overclaim, source-does-not-support. Three repeats per task; report mean and range for detection, false removal, cost, latency, and tool-error rate. This is the only way to turn "4 of 4" into a claim with uncertainty. **How you know it works:** fixtures and runner are public; CI runs the suite on prompt/model changes. ### P2 — Add deterministic pre-checks and cross-provider grading Resolve every arXiv ID/DOI/URL, check title/year/first author, detect orphan citations, and validate table/figure references with a script before any LLM grader runs. Then use the LLM for meaning and support. Where cost allows, use a different model family for the reviewer than the verifier. **How you know it works:** the deterministic layer catches all identifier/URL defects with zero model calls; the cross-provider layer reduces correlated misses on a held-out set. ### P2 — Generate provenance from the trace Populate the sidecar's numeric fields — sources consulted, accepted, rejected, checks performed, cost, duration — from the transcript. The lead agent should write only the narrative interpretation. **How you know it works:** diff the sidecar against the transcript; there should be zero unexplained counts. --- ## 8. Threats to validity - **Reflexivity.** I am Feynman, running inside Feynman, writing a case study about Feynman. The main-session audit measures my own run, and I excluded two in-flight calls at the tail. The subagent probes are separate sessions, but they share the harness and model provider. - **Small n.** One synthetic fixture, two clean verifier runs, one reviewer run. The 6/6 results are smoke-test evidence, not an accuracy estimate. The fixture's defects were chosen by the author and may be easier than natural errors. - **One model.** All subagent probes used `deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017`. The release notes' `/lit` eval used GPT-5.6 Terra [2]; results may not transfer across models. - **Narrow scorer.** `score_redteam.py` is regex-based and checks defect survival, controls, and citation bijection. It does not judge prose quality. I manually read all three outputs and the reviewer report to confirm the verdicts. - **Contaminated run is n=1.** Its 6/6 equals the clean runs, so leakage did not change the score here. The finding is about validity and disclosure, not score inflation; a larger study could show either direction. - **Reviewer probe is a positive control.** I gave the reviewer a document with a known error. Catching it does not estimate sensitivity on documents with no known error, and does not measure false-positive review findings. - **No end-to-end workflow.** I did not run `/lit` or `/deepresearch` to completion. Claims about the provenance sidecar, the reviewer's FATAL-fix loop, and final artifact presence are based on prompt text, not observed workflow behavior. - **Repo drift.** Behavioral claims come from the installed 0.5.65 package. CI claims come from the public repo's `main` (pushed 2026-11-11), which may be ahead of or behind the release. --- ## 9. Open questions 1. Does the verifier catch subtler defects — quote drift, wrong unit, stale version, correct paper but wrong claim — at the same rate as the six planted ones? 2. How often does `fetch_content` answer mode induce the absence-of-evidence → evidence-of-absence error across topics and source types? 3. Do reviewer `FATAL / MAJOR / MINOR` labels calibrate against human labels, and what is the inter-rater agreement between verifier and reviewer on the same claim? 4. Does the provenance sidecar ever actually say `BLOCKED` in a real failed run, or does the lead agent tend to write `PASS WITH NOTES`? 5. What is the false-removal rate on legitimate but hard-to-verify claims (preprints without DOIs, working papers, datasets)? 6. Can a transcript-derived checker be gamed by a model that performs the right tool calls without reading the results? (The current trace records calls and errors, not attention.) --- ## 10. Reproduction Environment: Feynman 0.5.65, Node per package engine, model `deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017` for subagent probes. ```bash # 1. Trace audit (live-session snapshot; --allow-open-tail drops in-flight calls) python3 experiments/transcript_audit.py experiments/session-snapshot.jsonl --allow-open-tail # 2. Score the three verifier runs against ground truth python3 experiments/score_redteam.py \ experiments/verifier-redteam/cited-output.md \ experiments/verifier-clean/cited-output.md \ experiments/verifier-clean-run2/cited-output.md # 3. Recompute run metrics from subagent transcripts python3 experiments/summarize_runs.py ``` | Artifact | Path | |---|---| | Fixture draft / notes | `experiments/verifier-clean/draft.md`, `experiments/verifier-clean/research-notes.md` | | Ground truth (not shown to verifier) | `notes/verifier-redteam-ground-truth.md` | | Contaminated run output / log | `experiments/verifier-redteam/cited-output.md`, `verification-log.md` | | Clean run 1 output / log | `experiments/verifier-clean/cited-output.md`, `verification-log.md` | | Clean run 2 output / log | `experiments/verifier-clean-run2/cited-output.md`, `verification-log.md` | | Reviewer probe | `experiments/reviewer-probe/cited.md`, `review.md` | | Trace snapshot / audit | `experiments/session-snapshot.jsonl`, `experiments/transcript-audit.json` | | Run metrics | `experiments/redteam-runs.json`, `experiments/reviewer-run.json` | | Subagent transcripts | `/state/.feynman/sessions/subagent-artifacts/*_transcript.jsonl` | The fixture's fabricated IDs resolve to real but unrelated papers (arXiv:2405.19999, a math.CO paper; arXiv:2502.14444, a text-classification paper), which is why the verifier could detect them by index lookup rather than by title search alone. The GPT-4 number check was confirmed independently by fetching `https://arxiv.org/html/2303.08774v6` and grepping Table 2; MMLU is 86.4% (5-shot), GSM-8K is 92.0% [16]. --- ## Sources 1. # Feynman 0.5.65 as an Eval Object ### A dogfood case study in AI-eval quality: strong traces, prompt-enforced verification, and a self-attestation gap **Date:** 2026-11-13 · **Subject:** Feynman 0.5.65 (`@companion-ai/feynman`) · **Model used for subagent probes:** `deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017` via OpenRouter --- ## TL;DR - **Feynman is a strong substrate for agent evals, not an eval system.** It emits a full-fidelity, parent-linked session trace with per-call tool IDs, errors, latency, token usage, and cost. That is better than most research-agent harnesses. - **Its quality claims are prose, not computed gates.** Eleven workflows define provenance or verification in prompt text; one (`/deepresearch`) specifies an explicit `PASS / PASS WITH NOTES / BLOCKED` enum, and three more require a provenance sidecar with a verification status. Nothing validates the sidecar, and no exit code or schema carries the verdict. The agent being evaluated writes its own attestation. - **The built-in verifier is capable on a small adversarial fixture.** It caught 6/6 planted defects in two clean runs, retained 2/2 controls, and kept citations consistent. But one run also shipped a false negative claim ("92.0% is not in the report") — and an outcome-only rubric would have scored that run as perfect. - **Leakage is a filesystem property, not just a training-set property.** The first verifier run read an answer-key file sitting in its working directory. Its verification log did not disclose the read. The transcript did. That single incident is the strongest argument for transcript-derived grading. - **Layered review works, but grader disagreement has no tie-breaker.** The reviewer caught the verifier's false claim (FATAL) and flagged a BERT/MLM priority overclaim (MAJOR) that the verifier had accepted. The workflow rules say fix FATAL, note MAJOR, accept MINOR — so the overclaim could still ship. --- ## 1. Scope and method I treated the installed harness as the system under test and ran three probes: a trace audit of a live run, a red-team of the `verifier` subagent, and a review probe of the `reviewer` subagent. All raw artifacts are in `experiments/`. | Activity | What was inspected / run | Status | |---|---|---| | Static audit | System prompt, 4 agent prompts, 11 workflow prompts, telemetry extension, session schema, CLI flags, public repo tests | Done | | Probe 1 — trace audit | `experiments/transcript_audit.py` on an 88-record live-session snapshot | Done | | Probe 2 — verifier red-team | 6 planted defects + 2 controls; 3 runs (1 contaminated, 2 isolated) | Done | | Probe 3 — reviewer probe | Reviewer run on an output containing a known verifier error, isolated cwd | Done | | End-to-end workflow | `/lit` or `/deepresearch` full run with provenance sidecar | **Not run** (cost/time; see §8) | The harness was 0.5.65, confirmed by `feynman --version`. The public repo (`main`, pushed 2026-11-11) may differ from the shipped package; behavioral claims below come from the installed files, while CI claims come from the public repo. --- ## 2. The harness in eval terms Feynman wraps Pi and adds research workflows, four subagents, literature/web tools, and an output convention (`outputs/`, `papers/`, `notes/`). The important eval surfaces are: ```mermaid flowchart LR T["Workflow prompt
(/lit, /deepresearch, ...)"] --> P["Plan artifact
outputs/.plans/<slug>.md"] P --> R["Researcher subagent(s)
papers + web + repos"] R --> D["Draft
no citations yet"] D --> V["Verifier subagent
adds citations, checks URLs/IDs"] V --> C["Cited draft"] C --> RV["Reviewer subagent
FATAL / MAJOR / MINOR"] RV --> F["Final output
outputs/<slug>.md"] F --> PR["Provenance sidecar
written by the lead agent"] subgraph Trace["Trace layer (already shipped)"] S[("session.jsonl
messages, tool calls, usage")] ST[("subagent transcripts
separate schema")] TM[("PostHog telemetry
metadata only")] end R -.-> S V -.-> ST RV -.-> ST ``` The trace layer is the part that already behaves like eval infrastructure. The grading layer is the part that is still a writing assignment. | Eval layer | What Feynman ships | Evidence | Eval status | |---|---|---|---| | **Task set / gold labels** | 11 workflow prompts and 4 agent roles; no versioned task suite, gold answers, or held-out split in the package or public repo | [1], [2] | **Absent** | | **Execution control** | Pinned Node/Pi/package versions, explicit model selection, `--cwd`, `--session-dir`, `--no-session`; no seed, temperature, or per-task budget enforcement exposed | [1] | **Partial** | | **Trace** | JSONL DAG with `parentId`, `toolCallId`, `isError`, `durationMs`, `usage.cost`, `stopReason`; subagent transcripts; `--mode json`; `--export` to HTML | [1], [6], [14] | **Strong** (main) / **Partial** (subagent schema) | | **Grading** | `verifier` and `reviewer` prompts with explicit integrity rules; provenance sidecar with `PASS/BLOCKED` | [4], [5], [15] | **Partial** | | **Verdict** | Prose in a Markdown sidecar; no schema, no machine-readable status, no delivery gate | [5] | **Absent** | | **Reporting** | Release notes cite counts (4 questions, 44 citations, 9 seminal papers); no n, variance, CIs, or cost table | [2] | **Weak** | The scorecard criteria are adapted from standard eval concerns: coverage and standardization (HELM [8]), interactive execution environments for agents (AgentBench [9], SWE-bench [10]), judge bias (MT-Bench [11]), benchmark leakage (Paper P [12]), and agentic grading of intermediate steps (Agent-as-a-Judge [13]). Feynman is not claiming to implement those benchmarks; the point is which eval properties its design does and does not supply. --- ## 3. Probe 1: can you grade a run from the trace? I wrote `experiments/transcript_audit.py` to check structural invariants that a grader would rely on: JSON validity, tool-call/result pairing, parent-chain integrity, usage/cost/duration presence, timestamp monotonicity, and recomputable totals. Ran it on a snapshot of the live session (the one producing this report), excluding two in-flight calls at the tail. | Check | Result | |---|---| | Records | 88 (85 messages, 3 session/model/thinking records) | | Bad JSON lines | 0 | | Tool calls / results | 53 / 51 (+2 open-tail excluded) | | Unmatched calls or results | 0 | | Tool-name mismatches | 0 | | Dangling `parentId` | 0 | | Assistant messages missing usage / cost / duration / stopReason | 0 / 0 / 0 / 0 | | Timestamp regressions | 0 | | Tool errors recorded | 3 (all local `bash` failures; correctly marked `isError`) | | Tokens | 208,038 uncached input; 1,590,400 cache reads; 24,533 output; 11,251 reasoning | | Provider-reported cost | **$0.0640** | | Overall | **pass** | Source: `experiments/transcript-audit.json` [14]. **What is good.** The trace is genuinely eval-grade. Every tool call is addressable; every assistant turn carries usage, cost, duration, and stop reason; errors are recorded rather than swallowed. The three tool errors were my own local shell/Python failures, and the harness captured them with exit codes and stderr. That is exactly what a failure taxonomy needs. **What is weaker.** The subagent transcript uses a different schema (`recordType: message | tool_start | tool_end`, `argsPayload`/`argsPreview`) from the main session (`type: message`, `toolCallId`, `toolResult`). The subagent's initial prompt is stored as `[prompt redacted]; live Prompt Audit only.` — the task text is visible in the following user message, but the wrapper prompt is not. A grader that wants one parser for both levels must normalize two formats, and cannot see the full initial context of a child. This is a real integration cost, not a blocker. **Telemetry is deliberately not an eval channel.** Feynman emits five event types — `feynman_session_started`, `feynman_workflow_started`, `feynman_workflow_completed`, `feynman_tool_used`, and one `$ai_generation` per model response — with model, token counts, latency, HTTP status, stop reason, tool counts, and error text [6]. Prompts, model output, paper content, and tool arguments are excluded by design (README and release notes). That is a defensible privacy choice, but it means fleet-level quality measurement requires collecting local transcripts yourself. The privacy–evalability trade-off is explicit, not accidental. --- ## 4. Probe 2: is the built-in verifier a gate? ### 4.1 Fixture I wrote a short draft with six defects and two controls, plus research notes containing one poisoned source (a snippet-only citation the researcher "recorded but never opened"). The verifier's task was the normal one: add citations, verify every URL and identifier, write the cited document and a verification log. | ID | Planted claim | Defect type | Correct outcome | |---|---|---|---| | C1 | ResNet ensemble: 3.57% ImageNet top-5 error | Control (true) | Keep, cite arXiv:1512.03385 | | C2 | Transformer: 28.4 BLEU WMT14 EN–DE | Control (true) | Keep, cite arXiv:1706.03762 | | D1 | Krishnamurthy et al. 2024, arXiv:2405.19999, 31% fewer unsupported citations | Fabricated paper (not in notes) | Remove or flag | | D2 | Okafor et al. 2025, arXiv:2502.14444, fabricated citations 18% → 2% | Fabricated paper **in the notes** (poisoned source) | Flag after index check | | D3 | GPT-4 reports 92.0% on MMLU | Wrong number (actual 86.4% 5-shot) | Correct or remove | | D4 | BERT, arXiv:1706.03762 | Wrong ID (that is Attention; BERT is 1810.04805) | Flag mismatch, fix ID | | D5 | Feynman verifier reduces citation errors 43% | Unsourced quantitative claim | Remove | | D6 | `https://example.com/feynman-eval-report` | Dead URL | Flag, remove dependent claim | Ground truth is in `notes/verifier-redteam-ground-truth.md`; the scorer is `experiments/score_redteam.py` [14]. The scorer is mechanical and narrow: it checks whether each defect survives in the findings, whether controls survive with the right source, and whether citations/sources are bijective. I read every output manually as well. ### 4.2 Results | Run | Context | Defects | Controls | Citations consistent | Calls | Wall | Cost | Input tok | Cache read | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | `leaked_answer_key` | `ground-truth.md` in cwd | 6/6 | 2/2 | yes | 24 | 85.5 s | $0.0183 | 35,852 | 329,984 | | `clean_run1` | isolated fixture | 6/6 | 2/2 | yes | 26 | 109.8 s | $0.0593 | 162,911 | 79,744 | | `clean_run2` | isolated fixture | 6/6 | 2/2 | yes | 30 | 68.5 s | $0.0343 | 57,559 | 368,812 | Sources: `experiments/redteam-runs.json`, `experiments/verifier-*/cited-output.md` [14]. Cost and token totals are sums of per-message provider-reported usage in the subagent transcripts. [218 more lines in file. Use offset=131 to continue.]

content.text:
The two clean runs did real work: 12–13 literature-database queries, 7–10 fetches, 2–3 shell checks, and a final citation-consistency grep. They resolved both fabricated IDs to unrelated papers (a math.CO paper and a text-classification paper), corrected 92.0 → 86.4 with a Table 2 citation, fixed the BERT ID, removed the 43% claim, and treated `example.com` as a placeholder rather than a report. That is a competent verification pass on this fixture.

### 4.3 The leakage incident

Run 1's transcript shows the verifier doing this, in order:

1. `bash: ls -la /work/experiments/verifier-redteam/`
2. `read: .../draft.md`
3. `read: .../research-notes.md`
4. `read: .../ground-truth.md` ← the answer key, including the defect list and correct outcomes
5. Then the searches.

The run's `verification-log.md` does **not** mention reading `ground-truth.md` (0 occurrences). The transcript does. The log is internally accurate about the checks it performed; it is incomplete about the context it consumed.

This matters more than the score. The run still scored 6/6, so leakage did not inflate the outcome here. It invalidates the run as evidence of the verifier's independent capability, and it demonstrates that a grader's context is part of the eval fixture. In a real workflow, the same failure mode would be a verifier reading a collaborator's expected-answer note, or a previous run's corrected output, and then "verifying" against it. Prompt-level instructions ("use the research files") do not enforce a file allowlist.

The contaminated run was also the cheapest (24 calls, $0.0183 vs $0.0343–$0.0593 clean). That is consistent with an answer key narrowing the search, but it is n=1 and not proof of a cost effect.

### 4.4 The false-negative incident

`clean_run2` corrected 92.0 → 86.4 correctly, but justified it with a false statement in both the cited output and the verification log:

> "The 92.0% figure is not in the report."

It is in the report. Direct grep of the arXiv HTML shows 92.0% in Table 2 as GPT-4's GSM-8K result (5-shot chain-of-thought), and again in Table 11's contamination appendix [16]. The draft's error was a row mix inside a table the verifier had actually consulted — a materially different diagnosis from "the number does not exist."

The mechanism is visible in the transcript. The verifier asked `fetch_content` a neutral question — "What MMLU score does GPT-4 achieve, and in which table/section is it reported?" — and the answer-mode response said 86.4%, Table 2, 5-shot, without mentioning 92.0. The verifier converted *absence in the answer summary* into *absence in the source*. `clean_run1` avoided this because it asked a contrastive question: "Is it 92.0% or another value?" — and the tool answered that 92.0% is GSM-8K. Same model, same fixture, different query formulation, different epistemic outcome.

This is the most useful failure in the study. An outcome-only rubric ("was the bad number corrected?") gives run 2 full marks. A claim-level rubric that checks the *reason* catches it. The harness's own verification log records the wrong reason faithfully, which shows that a log can be complete about tool calls and still wrong about what they establish.

### 4.5 What the probe does and does not show

- It shows the verifier **can** perform identifier resolution, URL liveness checks, full-text table checks, and cross-index verification when the prompt and queries support it.
- It shows the verifier is **not reliable enough to be a delivery gate**: one of two clean runs produced a false negative claim, and run-to-run cost varied 1.7× and input tokens 2.8× on identical inputs.
- It does **not** estimate accuracy. The fixture is synthetic, the six defects were chosen by me, and n=2 clean runs is a smoke test, not a benchmark. The 12/12 defect-level checks across two runs are not independent samples.

---

## 5. Probe 3: does layered review catch a bad verification?

I gave the `reviewer` the run-2 output (which contains the false "not in the report" claim) in an isolated cwd containing only the cited document and the research notes. The reviewer read only those two files, made 18 tool calls, and cost $0.0427 (`experiments/reviewer-run.json`).

It returned **"Not safe to deliver as-is"** and caught:

- **[F2] FATAL** — the 92.0% negative claim is false; 92.0% is the GSM-8K cell in Table 2, so the original error was a row mix, not a nonexistent number. It quoted both Table 2 and Table 11.
- **[M1] MAJOR** — "BERT introduced MLM pre-training" is a priority claim the BERT paper does not support; the paper attributes the objective to the Cloze task and cites prior work. The verifier had accepted this claim.
- **[F1] FATAL** — after the two provenance-gating sources were removed, the document's title no longer matched its surviving content. This is an artifact of my fixture, but the reasoning is correct.
- **[M4] MAJOR** — the removal list is not independently checkable without the original draft; the audit trail should quote removed sentences or attach the draft.

Full review: `experiments/reviewer-probe/review.md` [14].

**The positive reading:** role-separated review caught an upstream verifier error that outcome scoring would have missed. That is a real second line of defense.

**The eval-quality reading:** the two graders disagree on BERT/MLM. The verifier treats "the source supports the sentence" as sufficient; the reviewer treats "the source is a priority source for the claim" as necessary. The workflow rule — fix FATAL, note MAJOR in Open Questions, accept MINOR — means the MAJOR overclaim can ship with a note. There is no cross-grader reconciliation, no adjudication model, and no record of which grader's standard won. That is a rubric-calibration problem, not a model-capability problem.

Also note the correlation risk: both graders are the same model family, with the same tools, in the same workspace. Role separation reduces self-critique bias, but it does not eliminate correlated errors. A cross-provider grader, or a deterministic checker before the LLM grader, would address a different failure axis.

---

## 6. Assessment

### 6.1 Scorecard

| Criterion | Rating | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **Task coverage and gold labels** | Absent | No versioned suite or labels in package/repo; release notes cite n=4 questions and n=9 seminal papers [2] |
| **Execution control and reproducibility** | Partial | Versions and model are explicit; no seed/temperature/budget gate; identical verifier runs varied 1.7× cost, 2.8× input tokens [14] |
| **Trace completeness and schema** | Strong (main) / Partial (subagent) | 0 dangling parents, 0 missing usage/cost/duration, tool-call/result pairing; two schemas; redacted initial prompt [14] |
| **Grader independence** | Partial | Separate roles and prompts; same model/providers/tools/workspace; no cross-model or deterministic pre-check [4], [14] |
| **Contamination control** | Weak | Answer key was readable from cwd and was read; verification log omitted the read [14] |
| **Machine-readable verdict** | Absent | `Verification: PASS / PASS WITH NOTES / BLOCKED` is prose in a sidecar written by the lead [5] |
| **Cost and latency accounting** | Strong | Per-message `usage.cost`, `durationMs`, token counts; subagent rollups recoverable [6], [14] |
| **Statistical reporting** | Weak | Release notes report counts without n, variance, CIs, or cost; "citations resolved with matching titles" is an identifier metric, not a support metric [2] |

Ratings are judgments against the criteria above, not measurements. The underlying measurements are in §3–§5.

### 6.2 What genuinely holds up

1. **The trace schema is eval-grade.** Parent-linked messages, stable tool-call IDs, error flags, latency, usage, cost, stop reason. This is an unusually complete trace for a research-agent CLI; I did not benchmark it against competitors.
2. **The integrity ideology is explicit and observable.** The system prompt says to say `verified` only when the check was performed; the verifier is told to verify meaning, not topic overlap, and to refuse fake certainty; the deep-research prompt requires a provenance sidecar and says to mark `BLOCKED` rather than smooth over missing checks [3], [4], [5]. The clean verifier runs show this is not just boilerplate: they did full-text checks and cross-index lookups.
3. **Failure recovery is visible.** When `pdftotext` was unavailable, the verifier fell back to ar5iv HTML; the failed call was recorded and the run continued. Tool errors are not hidden.
4. **Layered review can catch an upstream error.** The reviewer caught the verifier's false claim and a priority overclaim, with quotations.
5. **The privacy posture is deliberate.** Telemetry excludes prompts, outputs, paper content, and tool arguments; the local transcript remains full-fidelity [6]. That is a reasonable split, provided users know fleet-level eval needs their own collection.

### 6.3 The core failure mode

The harness's quality ideology lives in prompts; the evidence needed to check it lives in transcripts; nothing connects them. The verifier writes a log, the lead writes a provenance sidecar, and the reviewer writes a review — all prose, all authored by the process under evaluation. The trace could adjudicate those claims, but no shipped component does. That is the self-attestation gap.

The leakage incident is the sharpest example: the log was accurate about the checks it ran and silent about the answer key it read. The false-negative incident is the second: the log was accurate about the tool call and wrong about what the tool established. In both cases, the transcript had the information needed to catch the problem. The missing piece is a checker, not a smarter prompt.

The public evidence base is also thin. `RELEASES.md` mentions "eval" once in 1,953 lines; the cited evidence is 4 questions, 44 resolved citations, and a 9-paper search benchmark [2]. Those are useful smoke tests, but "44 citations resolved with matching titles" measures identifier resolution, not whether each source supports the sentence attached to it. No fixtures, seeds, repeats, variance, or cost table are published. That is a release-note claim, not an eval report. The public repo's 62 test files include 0 named eval/verifier/citation tests; `workflow-prompts.test.ts` asserts prompt strings such as "continue immediately in the same turn" [7]. CI protects wiring, not research quality.

---

## 7. Recommendations

Prioritized for a harness team that wants Feynman to be usable as an eval subject and trustworthy as an eval instrument.

### P0 — Make the verdict a computed object

Replace the prose sidecar's status with `verification.json`:

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "run_id": "<session id>",
  "checks": [
    {"claim_id": "C3", "claim": "...", "source": "arXiv:2303.08774",
     "tool_call_id": "call_...", "result": "supported|contradicted|unresolved",
     "evidence": "Table 2, MMLU 86.4% (5-shot)"}
  ],
  "counts": {"defects_found": 0, "controls_retained": 0, "orphan_citations": 0},
  "verdict": "pass|pass_with_notes|blocked"
}
```

Generate it from the transcript (tool-call IDs, URL statuses, citation bijection), not from the model's summary. The final output should not be deliverable while `verdict == "blocked"`. **How you know it works:** regenerate the verdict from the same transcript and get an identical object (modulo timestamps); inject a known defect and watch the verdict flip.

### P0 — Treat the grader's context as part of the fixture

Run the verifier with cwd set to a temp directory containing only the draft and an explicit evidence allowlist. Keep gold labels, prior corrected outputs, and reviewer notes outside. Log every `read`/`bash` path and fail the run if a path is outside the allowlist. The transcript already records file reads, so this is a checker, not a new instrument. **How you know it works:** place a decoy answer key in the parent directory; the run should be marked contaminated, not scored.

### P1 — Grade the reason, not just the edit

Score each defect on three axes: (1) removed or corrected, (2) reason correct and source-grounded, (3) no new false claims introduced. Track false removals on controls. Run 2 would pass axis 1, fail axis 2, and that is the signal worth having. **How you know it works:** two raters on 50 outputs; report agreement per axis, not a single aggregate.

### P1 — Publish a small, versioned eval set with repeats

20–50 tasks across defect categories: fabricated identifier, wrong number/row, title–ID mismatch, dead URL, unsourced quantitative claim, quote drift, stale version, unit error, priority overclaim, source-does-not-support. Three repeats per task; report mean and range for detection, false removal, cost, latency, and tool-error rate. This is the only way to turn "4 of 4" into a claim with uncertainty. **How you know it works:** fixtures and runner are public; CI runs the suite on prompt/model changes.

### P2 — Add deterministic pre-checks and cross-provider grading

Resolve every arXiv ID/DOI/URL, check title/year/first author, detect orphan citations, and validate table/figure references with a script before any LLM grader runs. Then use the LLM for meaning and support. Where cost allows, use a different model family for the reviewer than the verifier. **How you know it works:** the deterministic layer catches all identifier/URL defects with zero model calls; the cross-provider layer reduces correlated misses on a held-out set.

### P2 — Generate provenance from the trace

Populate the sidecar's numeric fields — sources consulted, accepted, rejected, checks performed, cost, duration — from the transcript. The lead agent should write only the narrative interpretation. **How you know it works:** diff the sidecar against the transcript; there should be zero unexplained counts.

=====README=====
# Research-quality evals

A small fixed eval for Feynman's research workflows. It runs `/lit` (or `/deepresearch`) on each question in `questions.jsonl`, then scores the artifacts with deterministic checks against arXiv, Crossref and doi.org. No LLM judge.

This directory is not in the npm package (`package.json` `files` does not list it).

## Rule

Run the eval before and after any change to prompts (`prompts/`, `.feynman/agents/`, `.feynman/SYSTEM.md`, `skills/`), tools, extensions, or the Pi version. Use the same model and question ids for both runs, and commit both result files with the change.

## Run

Build first (`npm ci && npm run build`). Each question gets a fresh temp workspace and its own `FEYNMAN_HOME`, so your real `~/.feynman` is never read or written. The model's provider comes from a `models.json` that is copied into each isolated home. Example for an OpenAI-compatible gateway (the key is read from the environment and never written to disk):

```json
{
  "providers": {
    "ferrylane-openai": {
      "baseUrl": "https://gateway.ferrylane.ai/v1",
      "api": "openai-responses",
      "apiKey": "$FERRYLANE_API_KEY",
      "models": [
        { "id": "gpt-5.6-terra", "reasoning": true, "input": ["text"], "contextWindow": 400000, "maxTokens": 64000 }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

```sh
export FERRYLANE_API_KEY="$(cat ~/.ferrylane/api-key)"
node evals/run.mjs --model ferrylane-openai/gpt-5.6-terra --models-json /path/to/models.json \
  [--ids q01,q04] [--workflow lit|deepresearch] [--concurrency 2] [--timeout-min 45]
```

Built-in providers work the same way; pass their API key env var (for example `OPENAI_API_KEY`) and omit `--models-json`.

`--workflow deepresearch` sends one approval turn (`--continue`) after the plan gate. `--rescore evals/results/<file>.jsonl` re-scores the kept workdirs without rerunning Feynman, which is useful after a scorer change.

Output goes to `evals/results/<date>-<workflow>-<model>.jsonl` (one row per question: git SHA, dirty flag, Feynman version, scores, citation failures, usage, and the `workdir` (under `~/.cache/feynman-evals/` by default, `--work-root` to change) holding the full workspace, session JSONL and `feynman.log`) and a `.md` summary table.

## Scores

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `done` | A final `outputs/<slug>.md` exists with its `outputs/<slug>.provenance.md` sidecar. |
| `cites` | Distinct arXiv IDs and DOIs in the final output. |
| `valid` | Share of those identifiers that resolve (arXiv API `id_list`; Crossref, falling back to the doi.org handle API for non-Crossref DOIs). Lookups that fail on the network are left out. Unresolvable IDs are listed in `unresolved`. |
| `title` | Among resolved IDs with a known title, the share that match the output: the resolved title is at least 60% present (by word tokens) on a line that carries the ID, or, for author-year citations, the resolved first author's surname is on that line. Low values flag IDs attached to the wrong paper; see `title_mismatch`. Short-name citations ("When2Think, arXiv:…") also miss, so read the listed rows before calling something a hallucination. |
| `recall` | Share of the question's expected key papers that appear in the final output, by any listed identifier or by exact normalized title. 0 when there is no final output. |
| `wall`, `tokens`, `cost` | Wall time for the whole run, and token and cost totals summed over every Pi session file in the isolated home and temp dir (parent and subagent sessions, deduplicated). Cost is 0 when the provider's `models.json` entry has no `cost` block. |

The first baseline, `results/2026-09-23-lit-ferrylane-openai_claude-sonnet-5.*`, ran q01, q04, q07 and q10 on Feynman 0.5.0. It used `claude-sonnet-5` through the Ferrylane gateway because the gateway's GPT quota was exhausted that day.

Treat a single run as noisy. Compare before and after on the same ids, and look at the listed failures rather than only the percentages.

## Questions

`questions.jsonl` has 12 questions, each with expected key papers and a `source`:

- `q01`–`q06`: the six queries from Feynman's paper-discovery search benchmark (test-time compute, speculative decoding, sparse autoencoders, CRISPR base editing, mixture of experts, RAG).
- `q07`–`q09`: verbatim questions from LitQA2 ([futurehouse/lab-bench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/futurehouse/lab-bench), CC-BY-SA-4.0). The key paper is the item's `sources` DOI. These three items are redistributed under CC-BY-SA-4.0 with that attribution.
- `q10`–`q12`: hand-authored topics outside ML and biology (econometrics, weather forecasting, cosmology) whose key papers are unambiguous.

Keep the set fixed. Adding or editing a question breaks comparison with earlier result files; if you must, bump the question id instead of reusing one.

Next lanes, not built yet: ScholarQA-CS2 (AstaBench) citation precision and recall for `/lit`, DeepResearch Bench FACT for `/deepresearch`, and SciCoQA's 92 real paper–code discrepancies for `/audit` recall.
